    ]]>         Morocco’s surveillance state does not stop at Western Sahara — and Europe can no longer pretend not to know https://euobserver.com/241454/moroccos-surveillance-state-does-not-stop-at-western-sahara-and-europe-can-no-longer-pretend-not-to-know/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:50:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241454 As new evidence emerges of Moroccan spying on Sahrawi activists, including in Europe, European governments continue to deepen their security ties with Rabat without seriously questioning how those capabilities are being used.]]> In April 2021, I told The Guardian that Sahrawi activists were having their phones and internet connections hacked.

    At the time, we could describe what was happening to us. We could not see the machinery behind it.

    Five years later, Amnesty International’s new investigation, “We Start With the Verdict”: Inside Morocco’s Surveillance Machine, gives those warnings a disturbing new context.

    Amnesty describes a surveillance ecosystem involving spyware, physical surveillance, location tracking, informants, judicial pressure and smear campaigns. Western Sahara is not peripheral to its findings.

    The organisation devotes a case study to Sahrawi activists and reports that a former member of Morocco’s domestic intelligence service, identified as “Safir,” described Sahrawis and Riffians as priority intelligence targets, including beyond Morocco. Amnesty says it independently verified his identity, employment and key elements of his testimony.

    The report also contains forensic evidence involving Pegasus spyware and documents cases connected to Sahrawi activism that reached European territory.

    The people Amnesty examined are the tip of the iceberg. They are documented cases: people researchers could interview, devices they could examine, or targets for whom other evidence was available.

    Surveillance is secret by design. Most people never learn that their phones have been compromised, and most suspicious devices will never reach a forensic laboratory.

    That is why the chronology matters.

    Chilling effect

    On 8 April 2021, The Guardian quoted my warning that Sahrawi activists’ “phones and internet connections are hacked.” We were describing the symptoms years before Amnesty’s latest investigation exposed more of the machinery.

    But surveillance is not simply about collecting information.

    When a security service knows who an activist speaks to, where that person travels and what exists inside a phone, information can become power.

    Amnesty documents cases in which private information gathered through surveillance later appeared in media coverage and coordinated smear campaigns against human rights defenders.

    The organisation is careful: it could not independently establish the source of every piece of private material published. But it says the nature of some material raises serious concerns that surveillance-derived information may have reached media actors.

    For Sahrawis, that raises an obvious question: How does private information about activists move from their lives and devices into the public sphere?

    That question deserves independent forensic investigation.

    But Amnesty’s report should provoke another examination — this one in Washington and European capitals.

    For decades, Western governments have built close security relationships with Morocco around counterterrorism, intelligence cooperation, migration and regional stability.

    The question is not whether those relationships should exist. It is whether the West has adequately examined what happens to security capabilities once they are in the hands of its partners.

    Read more

    Sánchez and the EU have decided that Morocco relations are too big to fail

    Amnesty does not establish that every security capability Morocco obtained through Western cooperation was used against Sahrawis. The evidence does not support such a sweeping conclusion.

    It does, however, justify harder questions.

    What safeguards accompanied security cooperation? Who monitored end use? What happens when capabilities developed or acquired in an environment shaped by counterterrorism are directed toward peaceful human rights activism?

    That is the line separating security from repression.

    Western Sahara struggle

    The contradiction is especially striking because Sahrawi human rights activism has often relied on peaceful means: demonstrations, documentation, journalism and engagement with international institutions.

    Amnesty reports restrictions on expression and assembly concerning Sahrawi rights, alongside reports of arbitrary arrests, prolonged surveillance, restrictions affecting families and the dispersal of peaceful demonstrations.

    Europe has encountered similar contradictions in its relationship with Morocco.

    In June 2021, the European Parliament explicitly rejected Morocco’s use of border control and migration, particularly involving unaccompanied minors, as political pressure against Spain.

    Yet the same resolution emphasised the longstanding relationship and cooperation between the European Union and Morocco in counterterrorism, migration and trade.

    That contradiction should matter to Europeans.

    When democratic governments make another state indispensable for stopping terrorism, controlling migration or providing intelligence, they provide more than resources. They provide leverage. Eventually, fear of losing cooperation can make scrutiny of a partner more difficult.

    Europe has confronted another warning sign. In its response to the corruption scandal that engulfed the European Parliament, the Parliament itself denounced alleged attempts by Morocco and Qatar to influence lawmakers and staff through acts of corruption.

    Read more

    MEPs oppose including Morocco in Qatari corruption scandal

    These remain allegations. They do not mean that every European position favourable to Morocco was corrupt. But they demonstrate why foreign influence over democratic institutions requires serious scrutiny.

    European vs American foreign policy

    Western Sahara remains an issue on the United Nations agenda and is tied to a decades-long international process concerning the political future of the territory.

    That should matter to an EU that regularly invokes a rules-based international order.

    Morocco has rejected previous allegations concerning Pegasus and described earlier Amnesty findings as baseless. Amnesty says it provided Moroccan authorities with a summary of its latest findings before publication and invited a response but received none before the report was published.

    Those denials belong on the record.

    So does the evidence.

    The test of a human rights policy is not only how a democracy responds to abuses by its adversaries. The harder test is what it does when credible allegations concern a security partner.

    For Sahrawis, however, this story is older than spyware.

    For nearly half a century, generations of Sahrawis have lived through restrictions and documented abuses connected to political expression over the future of Western Sahara. Children have grown into adults watching what can happen when someone speaks publicly: surveillance, imprisonment, smear campaigns, pressure and fear.

    After all these years, what Sahrawis are asking for is not complicated.

    We are not asking the world to choose an answer for us. Nor should the outcome be written in advance in our favour.

    We are asking for something more elementary: Treat the Sahrawi as a free human being, capable of thinking, choosing and expressing a view about the future of the land he or she calls home without fear.

    It is easy to live in a democratic society, protected by freedom of expression and equality before the law, and then propose a political solution for a distant people who will have to live with its consequences every day.

    But a human question should come before the geopolitical one:

    Would you accept for yourself and your children a political order in which expressing your views about your homeland could expose you to surveillance, intimidation or punishment?

    A Sahrawi is not a number in a diplomatic file, a detail in a geopolitical bargain or a security problem to be managed.

    A Sahrawi is a human being, with a memory, a family, a homeland, an opinion and a future.

    After nearly 50 years, perhaps it is time simply to hear that voice as it is, rather than as others interpret it.

    Give Sahrawis one day without fear.

    One day to speak without surveillance, without pressure and without wondering whether their words will reach their phone, their workplace, their home or their family.

    Do not write the answer for them.

    Just let them speak.

    If any political solution is truly just, why should it fear the voice of the human being who will have to live under it?

    ]]>         Cut the EU budget and we all lose https://euobserver.com/241660/cut-the-eu-budget-and-we-all-lose/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:19:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241660 As national leaders call for massive cuts in the next EU budget, the parliament’s budget chiefs, MEP Siegfried Mureşan and Carla Tavares, warn that slashing EU cash now will undercut Europe’s competitiveness, security and social safety net for years to come.]]> When certain governments discuss the EU’s next seven-year budget, their first reflex seems to be: what can we cut? That is the wrong question. The real question is not how much the EU budget costs, but how much an insufficient budget will cost us all.  

    Economic benefits of EU membership are estimated to be two to six times the financial contribution of individual member states. For every euro we contribute to the EU budget, we can receive up to six euros in return.

    That is the power of investing together: European investment delivers more than fragmented national spending. And it does so with a budget of just one percent of EU GNI, while national budgets can reach 50 percent.

    The EU budget is not simply money transferred from national capitals to Brussels: it is an investment that creates value benefiting citizens through stronger economies, better infrastructure, food security, cutting-edge research, educational opportunities, regional development, and security.

    Ultimately, all member states benefit from the added value created by the EU, making the concept of ‘net contributors’ obsolete.

    Easing the pressure on national contributions is a legitimate objective, and it has a clear solution: an EU revenue reform. 

    Read more

    Von der Leyen joins MEPs in defence of EU’s €2 trillion spending plan ahead of summit

    The European Parliament supports the basket approach of the European Commission on new own resources and its proposals. It also proposed three additional options capable of generating substantial revenue by 1 January 2028: a digital service levy on major platforms (€25.2bn per year), a levy on online gambling (€3.9bn per year) and a crypto-assets-based own resource (€3bn per year).

    Our position is clear: large global companies that benefit most from Europe’s single market should contribute fairly to the EU budget that makes those benefits possible.

    Cutting the EU budget may look like saving money. But if it means weaker competitiveness, less social investment and a less secure Europe, we save nothing and taxpayers foot the bill.

    Read more

    EU 40% development aid cut would be ‘drastic betrayal’ of values, says top MEP

    The European Union’s common budget has not grown in real terms for 40 years. On the contrary, its purchasing power has been steadily eroded due to high inflation. The current EU budget has lost around 10 percent of its purchasing power compared to when it was adopted in 2020. 

    A more ambitious EU budget does not automatically mean that member states will have to contribute substantially more from their national budgets. When amounts are compared in constant prices and as a share of the size of the European economy – like with like – a more realistic picture emerges. 

    In terms of spending capacity, and without counting repayment of the Covid-19 recovery fund (NextGenerationEU), the commission’s proposal for the 2028-2034 budget would be below the relative size of the current 2021-2027 MFF at the time of its adoption.

    Even with parliament’s proposed increase for key EU programmes, member states’ contributions would still not substantially increase. 

    Read more

    Frugal EU states seeking budget cuts are shooting their own regions in the foot

    Let us not forget: Europeans benefit considerably more than their countries’ headline contributions suggest. The single market is the clearest example. By removing barriers between 27 economies, it creates opportunities and delivers growth that no country could generate alone. 

    By reducing the budget, the EU and its member states will have less capacity to deliver the economic and social benefits that citizens expect. We’ll have less cohesion, less competitiveness, a weaker agricultural sector, less global influence, reduced social investment and a much less secure Europe. And this also comes at a cost. A big one.

    Instead of “what can we cut” we should be asking ourselves, “how can we finance a budget that delivers more for all”.  

    If we genuinely want to use limited public resources efficiently, we must invest together. Economies of scale work for successful businesses, and they work for Europe.

    Siegfried Mureşan (EPP, Romania) and Carla Tavares (S&D, Portugal) are the parliament’s co-rapporteurs on the EU budget, also known as the multiannual financial framework (MFF)

    ]]>         Listen: Are student protests in France actually being fuelled by Mélenchon’s party LFI? https://euobserver.com/241671/listen-are-student-protests-in-france-actually-being-fuelled-by-melenchons-party-lfi/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:02:58 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241671 The biggest French high school student protests in two decades continue, as left-wing politicians join in criticism of the government.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    France has been seeing growing protests by high school and university students in recent weeks.

    The movement is continuing today with a fourth day of mobilisation. According to the government, the far-left opposition party is fuelling the protests. For Donald Trump, the movement is the result of mass migration and the presence of Islam.

    But what are young people actually protesting about? High school students’ anger has been building for some time. One of the tipping points came in June, when temperatures inside many schools rose above 35 degrees. Many classrooms had no fans, let alone air conditioning.

    And this happened in buildings that were already often in poor condition. Add to that the fact that absent teachers are frequently not replaced. The result was what you might call a general overheating — both literally and politically.

    Read more

    Listen: One year out, could the far-right win France’s 2027 election?

    The government, meanwhile, has accused the left-wing party La France Insoumise (France Unbowed, or LFI) of fuelling the protests. Some commentators have even suggested that the movement was orchestrated by the party from the beginning.

    There is little doubt that LFI is supporting the mobilisation and may be trying to benefit politically from it. But dismissing the protests as political manipulation risks ignoring problems that are well documented.

    As sociologist and child psychiatrist Laelia Benoit recently told Le Monde, assuming that high school students cannot think for themselves and must necessarily be manipulated by adults or political parties is, in her words, a way of denying them their ability to act politically.

    And many of their demands are supported by both parents and teachers. Teachers, for example, have long complained about the lack of replacements when they are absent.

    Read more

    How bad does it have to get for the ECB to save France?

    This is supported by the latest PISA report on France: 87% of French students — as well as school principals — said their school’s capacity to teach was affected by a lack of teachers.

    So young people are increasingly asking to be heard. Earlier this week, they put forward their demands, resulting in 10 concrete measures supported by both high school and university students.

    Among other things, they are calling for a major programme to renovate schools, more staff, a guaranteed €1 meal at university canteens, and higher housing benefits and grants so that students can live with dignity.

    So what is the government offering in response? France has opened an online platform in recent days where students can submit their demands. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said yesterday that the platform had already received more than 40,000 contributions.

    So for now, the government’s message is essentially: go back to class and submit your demands online. The prime minister then pointed to the additional €1 billion he has proposed for the education budget next year.

    And as for more immediate measures, he announced five areas of work that should begin at the end of October. They include tackling teacher replacements, improving schools’ material conditions, reorganising school timetables, reforming the university admissions platform which appears to be a nightmare, and thinking about how to give high school students a greater voice.

    Let’s see if that is enough to ease the protests.

      <title>Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/09/trump-investigate-lisa-cook-fed-governor</link>
      <description><p>US president renews his efforts to oust Cook despite supreme court ruling that her firing was unconstitutional</p><p>Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jun/29/supreme-court-trump-lisa-cook-ruling">a June supreme court ruling</a> that her earlier firing was unconstitutional.</p><p>Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/09/trump-investigate-lisa-cook-fed-governor">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Trump immigrant purge could cut social security for Americans by $2,000 a year</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-immigration-cost-social-security</link>
      <description><p>New report on economic cost of anti-immigration campaign projects 8.6% reduction in retirement payments by 2034</p><p>Elderly Americans can expect to lose an average of $2,152 in annual social security benefits each, a projected 8.6% reduction in their retirement payments, by 2034 and every year after as a direct consequence of the economic fallout from the Trump administration’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/series/ice-2-0-inside-trumps-new-immigration-dragnet">anti-immigration campaign</a>, if that carries on, according to a new report shared exclusively with the Guardian.</p><p>Already, US food prices are up, housing permits to build new homes are down – and even native-born Americans are losing out on potential jobs after the sudden exodus of 1.2 million foreign-born workers over the last two years as a result of Donald Trump’s policies, the report finds.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-immigration-cost-social-security">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Trump made ‘clear’ that media ban was due to critical coverage, court told</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/oct/08/trump-media-ban-hearing</link>
      <description><p>Lawyer for CNN, MS Now and Politico says Trump admitted he banned networks from White House over their coverage</p><p>Donald Trump continues to be the strongest witness for the media companies arguing that they were unfairly barred from the White House at his direction, a lawyer representing CNN, MS Now and Politico told a federal judge on Thursday afternoon.</p><p>The media coalition was in court asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order (TRO) he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. That temporary reprieve was scheduled to expire on Thursday, but district court judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said he would extend it until Tuesday and that he would probably rule on a motion for a preliminary injunction by that day. That means the White House will be forced to allow journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to continue accessing the building until at least Tuesday.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/oct/08/trump-media-ban-hearing">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Millionaire tax no more? Rightwing groups lead effort to repeal Washington state law</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax</link>
      <description><p>An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the 9.9% tax on earnings above $1m – who’s winning the fight? </p><p>Voters in Washington state will soon decide the fate of the state’s so-called “<a href="https://senatedemocrats.wa.gov/millionaires-tax-faq/">millionaire tax</a>” – a 9.9% income tax on earnings above $1m that was <a href="https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-signs-millionaires-tax-law">signed</a> into law in March and is now facing a conservative-backed effort to repeal it.</p><p>An <a href="https://leg.wa.gov/media/ucubvqsd/2026-summary-of-initiative-26-645.pdf">initiative</a> on November’s ballot aims to overturn the tax, claiming that the tax represents a slippery slope, and would eventually result in taxes for more than just millionaires. A <a href="https://no645.com/our-coalition/">coalition</a> of advocacy groups and unions opposing the initiative say taxing the state’s 20,000 highest-earning households could raise approximately $3.5bn in necessary annual revenue to fund core priorities like education and healthcare, and expand tax credits and sales tax exemptions.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSat, 10 Oct 2026 07:30:04 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: How does it work if I have €1 or €12,000 to put in?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/09/irelands-new-personal-investment-accounts-what-you-need-to-know/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/09/irelands-new-personal-investment-accounts-what-you-need-to-know/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 12:23:26 +0000Budget 2027 was, in keeping with the personality of the Minister for Finance Simon Harris, an exercise in soundbites – a little across a wide range of areas for everyone. The one exception was the personal investment account.

First flagged back in February, Harris finally provided some of the key details that will govern how people can use these accounts.

With the Central Statistics Office reporting strong savings by households and more than €170 billion sitting in bank deposits – most earning little or nothing in interest – he hopes the new accounts will encourage people to take a little risk with their money in the hope of better returns while providing funding that can help Irish businesses grow.

It’s a move that harks back to the great (and ultimately disastrous) exercise in widespread public engagement with the stock markets that was the flotation of Telecom Éireann.

The Government will hope fervently for a different outcome this time around. The last thing it needs come the next general election is disgruntled investors in a government-sponsored scheme who have lost some of their money.

What is a personal investment account?

The personal investment account allows individuals above a certain age to put some money into tax efficient investments rather than keeping it in cash on deposit at their local bank or with An Post or a credit union.

How does it work?

Harris said in the budget that people will be allowed to invest up to €12,000 a year in an account that can be invested in a range of assets. No tax will be charged on these accounts at all until your account balance tops €50,000 and, even then, tax will be levied only on any amount above that tax-free threshold.

The tax rate will be 1 per cent. There will be no capital gains tax, no income tax on any dividends or exit tax as applies on similar investment funds.

You can invest €1 or €12,000 in any year and you can invest it all at once or spread it out weekly or monthly across the year. If you do not use the full limit one year, you lose it. You cannot just carry over some of it to increase contributions the following year above €12,000.

There are no restrictions on taking your money out of these accounts either. You can withdraw some or all of your money when it suits you – subject to the limits of the actual investment product you choose.

These is not like the SSIA scheme where the State actually made contributions alongside you to the accounts. Here, the perk is really the fact that the first €50,000 in the account will be tax free.

When will these accounts be available?

Although the details were announced in the budget, they will not be available until July of next year, according to the Minister. This is to allow the Government pass the necessary legislation to set the scheme up and also time for the various investment houses to sort out what options they will offer consumers under the programme.

Who can invest?

Anyone over the age of 18 with a personal public service (PPS) number will be entitled to invest. While it has not yet been made expressly clear, the assumption is that they will have to be tax resident in Ireland.

Each person can have only one account.

There has been some interest from parents in opening these accounts for their children but, for now, no account can be opened in the name of anyone younger than 18. The Minister did hold out the possibility of the scheme being widened down the line to include children but not for now.

Tell me more about how the tax will work

The headline tax rate is very low – just 1 per cent – which certainly makes it sound attractive. However, you are not just taxed on the gains you make in any year but on the total amount in the account above that €50,000 threshold.

Let’s say you have €50,000 in your account at the start of the year and a strong investment return means your account balance rises to €56,000 by the end of the year. The 1 per cent tax is levied on the €6,000 above the €50,000 threshold – a tax bill of €60.

The following year, the investment return is not so good; in fact, your account loses value and by year end is worth €53,000. Even though you have made no money in that year, the 1 per cent tax charge will still apply to the €3,000 in excess of the tax-free threshold, so you will have to pay €30 in tax on an account that lost money.

That will take a bit of getting your head around.

If I’m going to have to worry about Revenue returns and paperwork, I’m not sure I’m interested

Good news, there will be no paperwork and no tax returns – at least not for you. It will be down to whichever fund manager you invest with to make the returns and ensure Revenue gets what it is owed.

Why are they doing this?

The Government is concerned about the amount of “dead money” sitting in bank deposits earning little or nothing. Inflation means this money is actually losing real value every year. The only “winners” are the banks who deposit it with the Central Bank at European Central Bank rates far in excess of what they offer their customers and then use it as a source of “cheap money” to fund their mortgage lending for which they charge you again, boosting their profits every step along the way.

It is also under pressure along with other states across the EU to do more to encourage investment.

If they are so keen to encourage us to invest, why the €12,000 annual limit? Other countries offer far more scope

True, other countries have significantly higher caps on the amount you can invest in such tax-efficient schemes. Why not here? In part, it’s probably a case of taking a fairly cautious approach to a very new type of investment. The Government really isn’t sure how popular this new account will prove to be and they are also wary of people who understand little about investment throwing money at high-risk products only to suffer losses.

And then there are the banks. They are doing very well off this €170 billion on deposit and will no doubt have let the Government know that an exodus of such funds would only lead to higher mortgage costs as banks had to turn to the market to raise funds for lending.

So what interest rate will the new scheme offer?

Now, see, this is the reason everyone is a bit nervous about this scheme.

This is actually one of the questions that was put to our team in the post-budget Q&A. But this is not a scenario where the State is setting an interest rate on your savings. And, in fact, Harris’s team has previously noted that they are not looking at offering the option to invest in cash funds – which are very low risk and operate a bit like a deposit account.

How well a person does under the personal investment account scheme depends on the return on their investment which will be determined by a host of factors – including your choice of investments.

Even with bonds, for instance, which do offer a set interest rate, your return is also determined by the underlying performance of the bond, which can itself rise or fall. You’ll definitely get your interest – unless the bond issuer defaults – but whether you get your original investment in the bond back depends on the market.

Ok, where can the money be invested?

We will get more detail when the legislation is published but what the Minister and his team have said so far is that you will be able to invest in publicly listed company shares, in bonds and in investment funds, including exchange-traded funds – funds that contain a basket of assets that can either mimic a wider index or encourage diversification. These investment funds include those offering exposure to commodities – things like gold or oil.

What will not be permitted is investment in areas of particularly high risk. This includes cryptocurrencies and leveraged investments like derivatives. Areas like private equity and investment in the shares of private companies also seem set to be ruled out.

I know little or nothing about such things. Who will advise me on where to put my money?

You are far from alone. Irish people in general are fairly risk averse when it comes to money, in part because they simply do not understand how markets work. The Government is promising a major financial literacy campaign and the consumer watchdog – the CCPC – has already set up a page to help people understand the concepts around investment. You can find that here. It has also put together a quick online self-assessment quiz with 8 multiple-choice questions to see how ready you might be to consider making investments.

Then, of course, there will be some information provided by the companies that will be selling these investments to you.

I presume they charge for that?

You can expect that they will. Fund managers are going to be keen to keep fees low on the products they sell to people under these personal investment accounts but the lower the charge, the less hand-holding you can expect.

The cheapest (and not necessarily the best) products will offer execution only. That means no guidance or personal interaction with the fund manager. It is up to you to do the homework; they simply sell the product if you decide you want it. The hope is that fees here will be around 0.5 per cent or even less.

If you want a more personal service, you can expect the fee will be higher – closer to 1.5 per cent per annum or more.

So is it a good idea?

Only you can determine if this is right for you. The focus on the Government side is to make these accounts as simple as possible to use. They will certainly offer you the chance to make more than you ever will on deposit but, yes, there is an element of risk involved.

It is not all or nothing; different products will have very different levels of risk. And, over time, such investments have outperformed the return on cash deposits.

As it stands, you are losing money on anything you have on deposit in the bank as inflation is now running at 4.1 per cent, way ahead of any interest you are being offered, even before Dirt is deducted.

You can contact us at OnTheMoney@irishtimes.com with personal finance questions you would like to see us address. If you missed last week’s newsletter, you can read it here.

]]><![CDATA[Never mind the ‘risk to humanity’, Anthropic’s IPO raises more prosaic concerns]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/10/never-mind-the-risk-to-humanity-anthropics-ipo-raises-more-prosaic-concerns/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/10/never-mind-the-risk-to-humanity-anthropics-ipo-raises-more-prosaic-concerns/Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:17:00 +0000Anthropic’s IPO (initial public offering) prospectus warns its AI model could cause a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity”.

Some investors may have more prosaic concerns, not least the amount of new stock coming to market.

Anthropic is expected to make its market debut next month, and it’s already clear that building a $2 trillion AI giant requires a very large cheque.

Revenue rose twelvefold last year to almost $4.6 billion but the company still recorded operating losses of more than $8 billion.

More strikingly, it envisages spending $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure in coming years. Extraordinary amounts of capital are therefore needed. Saudi Aramco’s $29 billion flotation in 2019 was the previous record, but SpaceX tripled it in June when it raised $86 billion at a $1.77 trillion valuation.

Now Anthropic will probably blow past even that, with plans to raise up to $100 billion at a valuation of about $2 trillion. And there’s more, with OpenAI expected to follow Anthropic with a trillion-dollar listing in early 2027.

The implications extend beyond the companies themselves. In a recent note, investment manager GMO warned that the sheer amount of new equity coming to market could become a catalyst for an AI bubble break.

For almost all of the past 20 years, US companies have bought back more shares than they issued. That is now going into reverse, with hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Oracle issuing shares to fund AI spending, a wave of giant IPOs adding new stock, and roughly $2 trillion of SpaceX shares becoming freely tradeable by June 2027.

GMO estimates that, if history is any guide, the resulting increase in equity supply could leave the market about 20 per cent below where it otherwise would have been over the following 18 months.

]]>Paul Scott<![CDATA[David McWilliams: We have just seen a perfect example of Ireland’s fiscal incontinence]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/10/david-mcwilliams-we-have-just-seen-a-perfect-example-of-irelands-fiscal-incontinence/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/10/david-mcwilliams-we-have-just-seen-a-perfect-example-of-irelands-fiscal-incontinence/Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Nothing focuses the mind like a hanging,” noted Samuel Johnson, according to his biographer James Boswell. The condemned man, realising that he has only a few weeks to live, focuses on what is truly important. The economic equivalent of this expression is: “Nothing focuses the mind like a hard budget.” Hard budgets make countries and organisations efficient, innovative, thoughtful and, by injecting financial discipline, ensure that decision-makers work through their options to get value for money. The hard budget in itself leads to better management, getting more from less, which requires more effort.

In contrast, a sloppy, bloated budget where money is not a problem will lead to waste, cynicism, cutting corners and the abandonment of accounting discipline. When money is wasted, the essential connection between the cost of something and the delivery of quality breaks down.

Without a hard budget, management becomes almost impossible and the corporation, organisation or country drifts, becoming gradually unable to deal with any shocks to the system that might lie ahead. Like someone who allows themselves to get out of shape, their muscles to weaken, and their weight to soar, the person becomes more susceptible to physical and potential emotional or psychological fragility.

Countries and corporations operate in a similar fashion. If they become addicted to easy money, particularly if that money is someone else’s, a gap opens up between reality and fantasy. The managers begin to feel that the money is theirs and they are entitled to it, creating a dependency. Successful management no longer revolves around the best use of the resources to achieve a specific outcome, but rather it becomes a smash-and-grab exercise centred on how much of the “easy” money the managers can get their hands on.

Without a budget constraint, the objective of management becomes size, not efficiency. The organisation becomes an extractive machine, extracting money from the central budget and, as that part of the organisation gets bigger, the fact of its expanding size means that it gobbles up more and more money, needing more every year just to stay still.

This is what has happened to the Irish State. It is a monstrously bloated organisation that has lost all sense of value for money and exists to gorge on cheap, endless cash that is cascading into the coffers from the US multinationals.

In development economics this process, whereby the State becomes hollowed out by too much rather than too little money, is termed the ”resource curse”. When an underdeveloped country without proper institutions finds a resource like oil, money flows in and it is often wasted, ending up in the pockets of the rulers, driving up costs for everyone else. The country ends up unbalanced – rich in parts but without the public infrastructure that the financial windfall could have paid for. Think Nigeria, Angola or Venezuela, where huge oil finds have not elevated the position of the citizens who own the natural resources of the country.

If these countries are synonymous with bad management, the exemplar of good behaviour is Norway, where the oil windfall has been invested judiciously and democratically for future generations, rather than blown on goodies for today.

Now look at Ireland’s equivalent of an oil find – the gusher that is the US multinational money, a spigot of cashflow, the product of clever tax arbitrage, which is flowing into the system to be pilfered by public sector management in a country that can’t even build a proper national rail system.

This week’s budget is a perfect example of the fiscal incontinence that a soft budget generates. First the Government flatters to deceive by announcing an overall surplus of about €9 billion next year. This looks great, but when you consider that the Department of Finance regards about €23 billion of the €34 billion in projected corporation taxes received this year as being transient, then we are in a different world. If we were to strip that out, our underlying surplus becomes a significant deficit of €13 billion to €14 billion for 2027; and, given commitments outlined in this budget, that deficit will widen to about €20 billion by 2029.

Even from a cyclical perspective, a country at full employment does not need any more money thrown at it – the economy is already bursting at the seams – and yet this week’s Budget 2027 is throwing a net €7.4 billion extra into an already bloated system.

New public spending efficiency taskforce to be established within three months

The Government presents it as cost-of-living relief. But the cost of living has risen because prices have risen. Throwing extra money at this problem will not cause prices to fall, but will cause them to rise, while the extra handout to soften the blow will simply increase dependency on handouts rather than cut prices and permanently. So you get the worst of all worlds: handouts which drive prices higher that are mistakenly put forward as a solution to high prices.

The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council’s analysis says spending is growing at double the pace of the Government’s own 5 per cent sustainable limit. Basically, our windfall is being spent rather than saved.

The lack of a hard budget also means that tough decisions are not taken, not just in the area of financial management but in organisational management too. Take, for example, this rotating taoiseach codology. With two bosses – one on the way out, the other on the way in – the lad on the way in is more important for tomorrow, undermining the lad in situ today.

Such management structure means that the incentive for all senior public servants and politicians is to curry favour with the next guy, not the guy in charge, thus undermining the guy in charge.

And by splitting the Department of Finance in two, with the Department of Finance and the Department of Public Expenditure, what’s the aim? Rather than have one department looking after the money, we now have two departments – and, critically, the Department of the Taoiseach, which used to be the nerve centre of final decision making, is now neutered because no one knows which taoiseach is more important: the incumbent or the next guy.

All the while global financial markets, the font of the windfall money that finances the large US tech companies, are becoming more and more nervous about the future.

]]>Mark Stedman<![CDATA[Woojer Vest 4 review: This vibrating vest might be the weirdest gadget I’ve ever reviewed ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/10/10/woojer-vest-4-review-this-vibrating-vest-might-be-the-weirdest-gadget-ive-ever-reviewed/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/10/10/woojer-vest-4-review-this-vibrating-vest-might-be-the-weirdest-gadget-ive-ever-reviewed/Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000I have tried out some unusual tech in my time. Bands that tap into nerves to help you lose weight or tackle insomnia. Sensors that encourage you to drink more water. Headphones that also act as a personal air purifier.

But a vibrating vest? That could be the weirdest yet.

The Woojer Vest 4 pitches itself as a “powerful and accurate 360-degree immersive experience”, a similar proposal to the acoustic therapy mat the company makes, but with a different target market. Instead of targeting wellness warriors, the vest is aimed at gamers, movie fans and music lovers who want to feel the audio, although you can use it for meditation too.

The Woojer Vest 4 takes audio and turns it into physical vibration, through six haptic transducers you strap to your body.

It doesn’t matter what the audio is – a movie, a game, Sabrina Carpenter on Spotify – as long as there is a bit of rumble to it. Low-frequency audio rumbles become vibrations and, in theory, you become fully immersed.

Sounds odd? Yes. Did it live up to the promise? Not really.

The device itself looks more like a life jacket than a wellness device or a gaming accessory, but I’ll keep an open mind.

Handily, it comes with instructions printed on the inside. Waist straps get tightened first, then the chest straps, and finally the shoulder straps.

Can a €1,100 high-tech vibrating mat help you sleep?

That was where the first issue became obvious. I’m shorter than average, so the distance between my shoulders and my waist is not quite what it would be for everyone. There isn’t much adjusting I can do on the shoulder straps to get that ideal “snug fit” the vest mentions.

That has knock-on effects. There are two pads on the chest, two on the back and two at the waist. Because of my lack of height, the chest vibration plates are, shall we say, interestingly placed, and the back vibration plates may as well not be there.

To get things working, you need to connect the vest to the Woojer app on your phone.

The unit sent for review needed a firmware update before I could get going, which requires the vest to be plugged in. That led to the second issue: there are two USB ports on the vest, one is on the back and the other on the front left side. Guess which one is for charging? The one I can’t reach without unstrapping the entire vest.

I unhook everything, plug the vest in and get going on the firmware update. Time for problem number three: it fails the first time and takes its time with the second attempt, so I shut it down, reboot the vest and try again. That requires a hard reset (there’s a small pinhole for that).

Ten minutes later we are updated and ready to go. Back on with the straps.

Now you can choose your audio source. The vest will work with everything from iPhone or Android device to PCs, consoles, smart TVs and VR headsets. If it is a phone, tablet or laptop, you can connect via Bluetooth and use either wireless or wired headphones for audio.

Other devices can be hooked up with cables, which effectively tethers you to your seat.

Music is the easiest to test. A wireless connection to the vest, wireless headphones, plus some bass-heavy audio makes for vibration overload. You can dial down the effect either through the app or the physical control panel on the vest. I made the mistake of cranking it up to the highest level on a particularly bass-heavy track and it felt like being hit in the chest. Would I buy a haptic vest for this experience? Unlikely.

Gaming seems like the natural use for the vest. Being able to feel the action instead of just seeing and hearing it would ratchet up the realism.

It didn’t quite work out like that. The haptics are based on audio rather than the game experience. The loudest sound triggers the biggest reaction. If that is the sound effects of the action, great; on some games it was the less crucial background noise, such as the rumble of vehicles and background music.

The problem is that it can all be a bit much after a while. Instead of making you feel more immersed in the content, it can get a bit muddy.

If I am running around a battlefield being shot at, I want the vibration pattern to reflect that. Shot in the chest? The chest plates should vibrate to reflect that. Instead everything blends together, and you can forget the vibration is even there. It is the same for movies and TV shows; sound effects and soundtracks are almost indistinguishable.

Some games have lag when connected to the vest via Bluetooth, even using the dedicated gaming modes. That makes the vibrating sensation distracting rather than immersive because it is coming too late. The settings don’t allow you compensate for it enough, focusing more on audio lag, so your best bet is to use a cable.

The most effective use for the vest is hooking it up to Calm or other meditation apps. But would you spend almost €500 to haul yourself into a vest and vibrate your way to inner calm?

Good

Connects to a range of audio sources, so you have choices about what you want to immerse yourself in. Works well for guided meditation and bass-heavy music, or stealth games that don’t overlay a soundtrack.

Bad

It just doesn’t seem too effective. It works on low-frequency audio – so anywhere there is a rumble, it translates to the vest and the end result isn’t targeted; it just becomes background noise.

The lag on some games devices makes the vest’s effects more of a distractions

Everything else

There are different modes in the app that can help tailor the experience. You can change modes, choosing between broad, focused, gaming and low latency – each has its own strengths. If you are using the vest for gaming, either low latency or gaming mode will be your best bet.

Verdict

The vest makes for an interesting accessory, but it isn’t as effective as I hoped.

Investment Scheme

Q: Why do you keep referring to it as the tax-free investment scheme? Is there deduction on contributions? It appears not so we have already paid tax on any money we pay into it.

From Mike

A: Unfortunately, there is no income tax deduction on contributions. The reference to tax-free investment is in referring to the income and gains arising on your investment in the scheme.

Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced there will be a tax-free threshold of €50,000. As such, where the value of your investment does not increase above €50,000, no tax should be payable.

Where you investment increased above €50,000, there is a 1 per cent tax on the value in excess of the €50,000. The 1 per cent tax will apply on an annual basis to the value in excess of €50,000 in that year.

There will be no requirement for you as the investor to engage with Revenue to make this tax payment should it arise, as this responsibility is expected to fall on the investment provider.

The maximum contribution limit is expected to be €12,000 per annum. We expect to see further details on this in the Finance Bill which is due to be released next Thursday. – RG

Childcare

Q: We are in a crèche in south Dublin and already pay well above the €735 cap. It’s five days a week which equates to 55 hours landing it in Band F.

The budget didn’t mention if banding impacts the cap, so will we be entitled to the €550?

From Paul

A: No, you will not. The €550 monthly cost relates to people availing of Band E care (creche care for up to 50 hours a week).

This year, Band E providers can charge €280 before the National Childcare Scheme subsidies of €2.14 per hour up to 45 hours. That subsidy brings the charge down to €183.70 a week, or €735 a month.

Band F providers can charge €336 a week under core funding. Even with the National Childcare Scheme subsidy, that still amounts to €239.70 a week, or €958.80 per month.

Housing

Q: We currently have a claim for Help to Buy in for the €30,000 amount. We have signed contracts but have not yet drawn down. Can we avail of the €35,000?

From Jack

A: The new, higher relief under Help to Buy kicks in from today but, as of now, it appears Revenue, which operates the relief, is unsure exactly what that means.

Certainly, going forward, any first-time buyer applying to the scheme will be able to claim relief of up to €35,000 towards the cost of purchasing a newly-built home, up from €30,000 previously.

They are also not yet able to clarify whether applications that have been approved but not yet drawn down can be amended to avail of the extra €5,000 in relief or not.

Social Welfare

A: There was no specific mention of graduate medicine fees. Childcare

Social Welfare

Q: When is the increase in fuel allowance coming in?

From Angela Parker

A: The fuel allowance has increased by €5 per week and we understand that this change will come into effect from January 2027. – BP

Minimum Wage

Q: From what date does the new Minimum Wage of €14.94 apply?

A: The new minimum wage will take effect from January 1st, 2027.

Capital Tax

Housing

Q: I submitted a claim for the Help to Buy scheme earlier this year and received the maximum €30,000. Am I entitled to the additional €5,000 announced yesterday?

A: Unfortunately, the increased amount is effective from today and will not be backdated. – RG

Investment Scheme

Q: Do you get to choose where your money is invested or does the Government supply guidance via a reliable broker?

A: The detail on how the investment accounts will operate has yet to be issued. We are expecting more detail on these accounts in the Finance Bill, which is due to issue on October 15th.

That said, the Minister did say that only eligible products, such as shares, bonds, investment funds and insurance based investment products, can be held in these accounts. – BP

Social Welfare

Q: Was there an inflationary increase added for the child benefit (€140 per child)? If not, why not?

From Anne Marie Murphy

A: Nope, there was no change in the €140 monthly payment under child benefit.

Why? well, you’d need to ask the Ministers, but I suspect they may have decided to concentrate their financial firepower in this area on childcare costs rather than child benefit. – DC

Investment Scheme

Q: If your portfolio is above €50,000 and you decide to sell them, are you subject to capital gains tax on the capital gain?

A: It is not anticipated there will be any capital gains tax on the disposal of your investment in the new Irish investment account. The proposal suggests that there will be an annual tax charge of 1 per cent on the value in excess of €50,000.

Income Tax

Capital Taxes

Investment Scheme

Childcare

Investment Scheme

Capital Taxes

A: Inheritance tax-free threshold are assessed against date of death, not probate or when the inheritance is received. So, in this case, where the person died earlier this year, it is the pre-budget thresholds that will apply. – DC

Thank you

We are ending our live Q&A now. Anyone with further queries can contact Dominic Coyle at dominic.coyle@irishtimes.com and he will endeavor to provide answers in his weekly Q&A column.

Thank you for joining us.

Geologists can estimate accurately when Norway’s oil and gas reserves will expire.

In Ireland, we have no line of sight. We’re completely in the dark. The tax windfall could go on for another decade or could fall off a cliff tomorrow. Even the chief financial officers of Apple, Microsoft and Eli Lilly, the State’s three biggest taxpayers, don’t know.

And yet we’re funnelling a huge amount of this windfall (€6 out of every €7) into everyday spending, into income tax breaks, into rent supports, stuff that won’t easily be resiled from.

We’re probably the only State in the world that bases its budgetary arithmetic on a handful of multinationals and the revenues they generate outside Ireland.

“The budgetary arithmetic is constructed on the crucial assumption that corporate profitability continues to expand; any decline in profitability could put a (potentially large) dent in corporate tax revenues,” the Department of Finance said in a report released with Budget 2027 on Tuesday.

If we had saved the windfall element of corporation tax since 2015 – approximately 50 per cent of annual receipts – the State would now have a war chest of €130 billion, capable of generating about €10 billion annually in interest (a typical stock market return).

Government ‘will need to borrow’ for new wealth funds as spending rises at fastest rate in EU, says watchdog

This would be enough to do away with the Universal Social Charge (USC) in one fell swoop, without having to raise tax elsewhere.

So much of Ireland’s tax system is still on an emergency setting from the financial crash, USC being the most obvious example.

The tax-free inheritance threshold of €420,000 and the 33 per cent capital acquisitions tax (CAT) that applies thereafter compares with a pre-crash threshold of €542,000 and CAT of 20 per cent.

Of course Ministers will point to the political straitjackets they find themselves in, the realpolitik of a modern democracy.

If Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced this week that he was planning to save €17 billion of the expected €34 billion in corporate tax this year in the midst of a cost-of-living crisis, he would, like Michael Collins, have been signing his own political death warrant and that of Fine Gael.

And therein lies the problem.

Big change requires a break from the sort of electoral budgeting, the winners and losers narrative, that we’ve had to date. A break from the firefighting, from the sticking plaster measures.

We’re apparently rolling in money, but everyone feels poorer and nobody is happy

We’ve had four years of energy credits and we still have the most expensive electricity prices in the European Union (EU). The credits are not a solution so much as a stop-gap. It’s the same with housing. The more money we spend on the housing assistance payment and other rent supports, the more there is a general erosion in affordability.

One senior figure said that Ireland acts like a poor country, spending money as it gets it, gambling on the back of future revenues, when it is actually a rich country that should be thinking more strategically about its wealth.

“Why don’t we feel the budget day numbers? One reason is that it’s going on hiring more staff across the public sector,” he said.

General government spending jumped by 54 per cent between 2019 and 2025, from €86.9 billion to €133.8 billion, facilitated by record corporate tax receipts.

At the same time, employment in the public sector rose by almost 80,000, from 339,000 to 417,000.

“If the Government thinks this (the additional employment) is warranted, it should be paying for it with money it can depend on,” the senior figure said.

Public spending hits record level as watchdog sharply criticises Budget 2027

The Government seems to have shelved any semblance of a plan to widen the tax base and seems content to play the game with the chips it gets from Corporate America.

Experts disagree on whether Ireland has what’s known in economics as “Dutch Disease” – where a sharp increase in wealth in one sector (usually from the discovery of oil or gas) bids up prices, creating cost challenges and a gradual loss of competitiveness.

The National Competitiveness and Productivity Council says Ireland is now “firmly part of the high-cost cluster in Europe”, with labour costs rising faster than the EU average since 2021. In the three years after the pandemic, labour costs rose faster than in the 13 years previous.

After playing a stellar role in financial crisis, Ireland now sits in an ivory tower at one remove from the financial zeitgeist: debt and fiscal constraint.

Tax receipts more than cover spending, resulting in healthy budget surpluses, while Government debt as a percentage of gross domestic product is now under 35 per cent. In the UK (in 2025) the equivalent was 101 per cent. In France, it was 115 per cent. In the US, 121 per cent.

There’s a good chance we’ll come to regret this period as a missed opportunity.

]]>MediaProduction<![CDATA[Who’s hiring and who’s firing in Ireland’s technology sector? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/whos-hiring-and-whos-firing-in-irelands-technology-sector/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/whos-hiring-and-whos-firing-in-irelands-technology-sector/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000The announcement by Stripe last week that it would create 200 jobs at its Dublin headquarters was a welcome piece of good news for the tech sector in Ireland.

Ireland’s tech sector has been a driving force for the economy in recent years, but as companies try to cut costs globally and keep shareholders onside, the threat of job losses has returned. That has caused understandable nerves in the sector. The memory of the “tech wreck” of 2022 and 2023 is still fresh, when the cuts came fast, and they came with big numbers. Could we be heading for another?

The headline increase was driven by a surge in the price of energy products, including electricity, gas and other household fuels, which were up by 13.7 per cent in the year to September.

Home heating oil prices rise almost 60%

Petrol prices, meanwhile, increased by 14 per cent in the 12 months to the end of September, with diesel up by 22 per cent.

Energy prices have soared this year in the aftermath of the US-Israeli war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Dermot Daly, EY Ireland consumer products and retail lead, said the jump in energy prices in the latest CSO data is “particularly noteworthy”.

“Consumers have shown resilience – household spending is likely to grow 2.5 per cent after inflation this year – but many will have to prioritise essential purchases while taking a more considered approach to discretionary spending,” he said.

“As we move closer to the important Christmas trading period, retailers will be hoping that consumer spending remains resilient despite ongoing cost pressures.

The Central Bank is now forecasting headline inflation to average 3.4 per cent in 2026, moderating to 3.1 per cent in 2027 and 2 per cent in 2028.

However, in its most recent quarterly economic bulletin, the bank warned that there were significant upside risks to these inflation projections given the uncertainty over the path of the conflict in the Middle East.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM Ireland and RSM UK said last week that the higher energy prices will likely feed into other areas.

“Utility bills will continue to reset higher, keeping energy inflation sticky throughout 2027,” he said. “At the same time, the sustained rise in energy prices this year means it’s increasingly likely that food, manufactured goods and other energy-intensive services such as airfares inflation will pick up pace in the coming months.”

]]>SupawadeeAdam<![CDATA[Bank of Ireland contains losses on US leveraged finance loans with insurance deals ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/financial-services/2026/10/08/bank-of-ireland-contains-losses-on-us-leveraged-finance-loans-with-insurance-deals/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/financial-services/2026/10/08/bank-of-ireland-contains-losses-on-us-leveraged-finance-loans-with-insurance-deals/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 13:47:16 +0000Bank of Ireland has contained losses in its US leveraged acquisition loan book through insurance deals that shared the risk with specialist investors.

The leveraged acquisition loan portfolios were typically issued as part of a club of banks to companies internationally going through a buyout or capital reorganisation.

The bank decided last February to wind down its US leveraged acquisition finance unit, which had a portfolio of €2.5 billion a few years ago. That had fallen to €1.2 billion by the end of June. It will be wound down over three years.

Bank of Ireland entered into transactions in December 2021 and May 2024 that saw specialist institutional investors take on credit risk for millions of euro of potential losses on the portfolios of loans. These deals, carried out by issuing bonds, are known as significant risk transfer (SRT) deals.

Bloomberg reported on Thursday that ArrowMark Financial, a long-standing investor in SRTs, now values the remaining bonds from Bank of Ireland’s 2021 transaction at around 34 US cents on the dollar. This reflects the losses being borne by the bondholders from a surge on problem loans in the US leveraged finance market in recent times, driven by a spike in interest rates following an extended period of cheap finance.

Meanwhile, First Trust Alternative Opportunities Fund marked down its outstanding position in a similar SRT issued in 2024 to 91 cents, Bloomberg said.

A spokesman for Bank of Ireland, which is led by chief executive Myles O’Grady, declined to comment.

Under SRT transactions, the original bank lenders typically face initial losses on a problem loans, with SRT investors assuming an agreed amount of potential losses thereafter. These insurance deals allow banks to free up some expensive capital that they would otherwise have to hold against the loan portfolios.

Bonds relating to both the affected transactions paid coupons – or interest – of more than 13 per cent a year, reflecting the perceived risk involved at the outset.

Bank of Ireland said in its 2024 annual report that specific corporate defaults in the US acquisition finance portfolio drove a €127 million group loan loss charge that year. Defaults in this business made up a portion of €110 million of impairment losses booked in its non-property small and medium enterprise (SME) and corporate loan portfolio in 2025, according to its latest annual report.

The opacity of the structures and private nature of the market means it’s often difficult to establish the magnitude and frequency of these writedowns.

Still, SRT issuance has boomed in recent years, enabling mostly European and North American lenders to offload risk tied to $1 trillion (€890 billion) in loans and to release capital for new lending or shareholder payouts. – Additional reporting, Reuters

]]><![CDATA[Is the State’s new investment account going to be a good deal?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/08/is-the-states-new-investment-account-going-to-be-a-good-deal/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/08/is-the-states-new-investment-account-going-to-be-a-good-deal/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 12:12:00 +0000Is the State’s new investment account going to be a good deal? The announcement of key details in the budget has certainly attracted renewed public interest. But it is essential to understand the fundamentals of the scheme to judge how it might fit in to your personal financial plan. And in assessing this, investors need to realise that they are going to be largely on their own.

Most of those providing the plans – the big banks and insurance companies initially – are likely to follow a low-charge model, meaning they will not offer personalised advice. Instead people will get some online essentials about the various plans on offer and choose – via a bank app, for example – what level of risk they wish to take.

It will, of course, be open to potential investors to seek personalised guidance from an adviser, or sign up for a more bespoke scheme, but this will cost more. All kinds of funds offered by brokers will be “wrapped” in the new scheme, in other words constructed to take advantage of it.

But charges here will be higher. As the offers develop, options are likely to grow. But cheap and cheerful will be the hallmark of the initial approach when the big players kick it off next July.

The tax-free nature of the scheme on holdings up to €50,000 is attractive. But still, there are some steps to assessing whether taking part works for you.

The first key point is that the return has to be greater than that available on a risk-free asset such as a bank account. Many people have cash currently in demand accounts with the main banks offering very low returns. But they could get 2 to 3 per cent – or even a bit more – if prepared to move into a savings account which might require notice on withdrawals.

Lower-than-expected annual €12,000 investment account limits may curb take-up

Returns are subject to deposit interest retention tax (Dirt) at 33 per cent, so that needs to be deducted – a third of your interest goes to the taxman.

Traditionally, stock markets have offered significantly higher returns than this. The Stoxx Europe 600 index, for example – the kind of index which an investment under the scheme might be based on – has had an average return of 8 per cent over the past 20 years. Most European indices has returned at least 6 per cent over that period.

But the Stoxx index lost 12 per cent in 2022, as inflation surged following Russia’s full scale invasion of Ukraine. So the first thing for new investors to understand is that you have to be able to ride out the bad years and let the averages – the fact that equities tend to go up more years than they go down – lead to gains over time.

Of course we cannot be sure that stock markets will behave in future like they did in the past. And we don’t know what markets will look like next July when the funds are launched, but this will need to be taken into account.

A bursting of the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble or the wider knock on to bond markets from rising interest rates present risks.

Investors will have a broader exposure than those who put cash into Eircom when it floated in 1999, but its initial rise and then fall as tech shares were hit as the dot.com bubble burst is worth noting, nonetheless.

If investors are happy to lock in their money for a period, then history suggests that equity market will beat deposits. Their next key call will be how much risk to take. At least initially, funds are likely to be marketed as high, medium and low risk. The latter will put some cash in traditionally less volatile areas such as bonds (though these have been on a volatile run of late).

This is where the lack of advice on basic products could be difficult for new investors in choosing where to put their money. We will have to see how the offers line up, but the funds will make more sense for those willing to take a somewhat higher level of risk and thus get a higher return over time. You need to beat the bank account return and also take into account the costs of the scheme.

The key cost most investors will need to factor in is whatever the provider is charging to offer the service. The indications are that there will be an effort to keep costs on basic offers down below 0.5 per cent – but remember this is a charge on the total value of the fund. There are also likely to be products offer bespoke advice but with higher charges, likely more than 1 per cent.

A charge of 0.5 per cent would be €100 on a €20,000 pot, while 1 per cent would be €200. This may not sound like a big difference. But over time charges matter as more money is taken out of the pot and there is a cumulative hit. Over 10 years the difference between a 0.5 per cent fee and a 1 per cent one on a €50,000 pot would be well in the thousands of euro.

The best hope for investors is that the big banks and their investment arms will keep the charges low to try to hold on to money which people are moving from deposits with the same group. But charging structures will be vital to assess. And these low-cost products leave investors making their own decisions.

The next bar to jump is the State tax. A big attraction of the scheme is that normal taxes on investment – capital gains tax and the taxes paid on exchange-traded funds – will not apply. It is only on pots of more than €50,000 where the new 1 per cent charge on the balance above this figure applies. So a couple could have two accounts summing to €100,000 and pay no tax.

Like charges from the provider, the 1 per cent will be significant for bigger investors. If an investor has saved, say, €100,000 then the annual charge will be €500 (1 per cent of €50,000).

As with charges, this eats away at the pot over time. And – crucially – this will be charged in good years and in bad – in other words in years when the value of your investment falls you will still pay the 1 per cent charge on balances of more than €100,000.

In Sweden this type of levy was initially charged on the whole sum saved and this led some experts to conclude that the tax advantage offered by the products – which like Ireland spared investors from capital gains tax – was limited.

The key attraction, they said, was simplicity, the fact that the provider does all the administration and also avoiding having to pay a big capital-gains bill all at once when the investment was sold.

More recently Sweden also introduced a tax-free scheme this year, which means a pot of up to €27,000 will not face a levy. The tax on amounts above this is 1.065 per cent.

For Ireland, investors will need to realise that the sums change significantly when savings become subject to the 1 per cent charge. There will probably still be tax advantages, but they will be narrower on the part of the fund exceeding €50,000 – and having to pay no matter how the fund performs is significant in bad years.

The bottom line is that the new investment vehicle is better suited to slightly riskier investments which offer a higher potential return. It also requires the investor to understand the risks and the need to be able to leave money where it is – if necessary – to recover from bad years. And to understand the impact of the 1 per cent charge on larger sums and the fees on all investments.

For many it may still offer an attractive part of a wider savings plan, which might also include a pension plan, some highly tax-incentivised additional voluntary contributions and some money in the bank for the “rainy day” when funds might be needed quickly.

But understanding what is and what is not on offer is vital. Just because this is a “State” scheme does not mean any kind of guarantee is on offer. It is not a special savings incentive account Mark 2. As the radio ads say. investments can fall as well as rise.

RTÉ reached a multi-year funding deal with the previous government in 2024. Under the agreement, the broadcaster would receive €725 million over three years: €225 million in 2025, €240 million in 2026, and €260 million in 2027.

TG4 and Screen Ireland budget funding amounts to ‘cut’ in real terms, industry warns

In the Dáil, the Taoiseach said a dispute “would be unwarranted given our willingness to talk”.

Some €1.2 billion has been set aside in the budget for a public pay deal. Martin said “there is no basis for industrial action or for disrupting people in education, health or anything else when this platform is there as a basis for negotiation on a new pay agreement”.
