]]><![CDATA[Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/06/consumers-can-save-up-to-50000-tax-free-in-new-personal-investment-accounts/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/06/consumers-can-save-up-to-50000-tax-free-in-new-personal-investment-accounts/Tue, 06 Oct 2026 15:44:46 +0000People will be able to put €12,000 a year tax-free into the Government new personal investment accounts, Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced in his Budget 2027 speech.

The accounts will feature a low tax rate of just 1 per cent. However, this tax will be levied on any amount in the account over a tax-free threshold of €50,000, not just the profit the account made over that year.

This holds out the prospect of people paying tax on their savings in years when they lost money simply because the balance of their account was above the €50,000 tax-free threshold.

Harris said the new accounts will be available from July 1st next year. About €170 billion is currently on deposit in Irish bank accounts, with the Minister having previously described that money as “sitting idle”.

Alongside the new accounts, the Minister announced a financial literacy campaign. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) has set up a webpage that will allow people to read up about issues around investing, and the choices available.

It also offers a quick multiple choice self-assessment quiz that allows consumers to assess their investment readiness.

Irish households hold just 2.3 per cent of their financial assets in direct investments such as listed shares and debt securities, compared with an EU average of approximately 7.5 per cent.

Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day

The new scheme has been designed to encourage people to move their savings into market investments.

“The long-mooted investment account is an important step towards making long-term investment more accessible,” said Cróna Clohisey, director of members and advocacy at Chartered Accountants Ireland. “Now that the broad design has been announced, Government should move quickly to finalise the legislation, systems and guidance so that financial service providers can establish these accounts and people can begin using them.

“It is critical that there is no delay to the introduction timeline of mid-2027,” she said.

Michael Healy, chief executive of IG Consumer, said the Government had missed the chance to get Irish people investing.

“While the decision to set the tax-free threshold at €50,000 is better than we expected, it is a small victory within a fundamentally flawed model. The €12,000 annual contribution limit is far too low if the ambition is to get people investing seriously and building meaningful long-term wealth.

“But the bigger problem is the proposed 1 per cent annual tax on investments above the threshold,” said Healy. “Taxing the value of an investment rather than the return it generates means someone could face a tax bill even when their investments have fallen in value – effectively paying tax on losses. That is the wrong principle for an account designed to encourage people to invest.”

Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income

Robert Dever, head of tax at Eversheds Sutherland, agreed. The Government he said had adopted a cautious approach to the new scheme. “For a lot of taxpayers, in the long term, it will probably be more tax efficient to maximise tax relief arising on pension contributions before contributing to an investment account.”

However, Rory O’Brien, head of wealth management, Dublin, at Baker Tilly Ireland Wealth was more upbeat.

“On the whole, the new Irish Investment Account looks like a fantastic opportunity for those looking for better returns from the investment markets over the medium to long term to do so without being harshly punished when their investments do well. The opportunity for younger investors to start small and build up to the 50k without CGT is very positive and l would expect those looking to build deposits, to consider this as a viable option.”

The Government also announced a lowering of the rate of tax under the “deemed disposal” or exit tax regime that applies to investors in products currently available in the market.

Budget 2027 main points: Minimum wage to rise 79 cent; €12,000 per year limit for investment scheme

Last year, as part of Budget 2026, the deemed disposal tax rate was reduced from 41 per cent to 38 per cent. In 2024, a report by the Department of Finance into the funds sector advised the deemed disposal rule should be ended for exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and investment funds.

Exit tax is levied on profits when an investment is cashed in. Deemed disposal sees that tax levied every eight years after an investment is taken out, even if the investment is not cashed in.

Chartered Accountants Ireland’s Cróna Clohisey said it was “extremely disheartening that the eight-year deemed disposal rule remains. It has no place in a modern Irish investment landscape.

“Requiring people to pay tax on gains they have not realised undermines the benefits of long-term investment, adds unnecessary complexity for individual investors, and contradicts the wider Government drive to foster retail investment and encourage greater financial literacy.”

Irish Funds chairwoman, Andrea Kelly welcome dthe three point cut in the rate of tax but said the lack of any clear path to phasing out deemed disposal was “deeply disappointing”.

“The Government should now use the Finance Bill to provide the certainty that was missing from the Budget,” she said.

New accounts

Anyone over the age of 18 who is resident in the State and holds a PPS number can invest in the new personal investment scheme, but they can only have one account.

Eligible investments will include listed shares, listed bonds, financial instruments traded on a regulated market and a range of investment funds suitable for retail investors, including ETFs.

Investors will not be permitted to invest in what are deemed highly complex and risky products, including derivatives and crypto assets.

Catch up with all your Budget 2027 news here

There will be no minimum holding or lock-in period, and moving investment accounts between providers will be allowed, where possible, on a tax-neutral basis.

Any tax due will be calculated and paid at source by the companies providing the investment funds available under the scheme.

What is not yet clear is how much providers will charge for the products they offer.

Harris first announced his intention to introduce a new form of consumer-friendly investment account back in February.

He has returned to the theme regularly since then but, until Tuesday, had declined to confirm the amount that could be put into such accounts each month or year, the threshold above which the funds will be taxed, or the rate of taxation.

Harris’s department had examined similar types of accounts operating in other countries. Ultimately, it opted largely for the Swedish model despite strong industry lobbying in favour of the rival UK individual savings account (ISA) model.

   <title>Selenskyj sieht „Geschenk an Putin“</title>
   <description>Nachdem US-Präsident Donald Trump am Freitag eine Vereinbarung zur Lieferung von Hunderttausenden Tonnen Diesel aus Russland verkündet hatte, kam scharfe Kritik aus Kiew.    <description>Die seit Wochen andauernden Wald- und Flächenbrände in Indonesien hüllen Südostasien vielerorts in dichten Smog.     <item>

Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar.

They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time.

🔴Ubili kozę na zapleczu. Wkrótce decyzja sądu, zastanawia ruch prokuratury

Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków…

— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 7, 2026

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.

After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.

The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF

 

A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.

However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.”

Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.

The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.

Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS).

Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026

Not all cases involving illegal animal slaughter have been treated as causing low social harm. Last month, a court in the town of Limanowa convicted three men for carrying out illegal halal ritual slaughter and selling unapproved meat.

The main suspect, a Polish man, was found guilty of overseeing the operation, while two Azerbaijani nationals were convicted of helping distribute the illegal meat. The verdicts can still be appealed.

Although it has relatively small Muslim and Jewish populations, Poland is one of Europe’s biggest producers and exporters of kosher and halal meat.

Almost a third of Poland's meat exports are halal and kosher, making it one of Europe's leading producers.

Having fought off attempts by the ruling party to ban ritual slaughter, the industry is now hoping to expand further to cater to a growing market https://t.co/duOJTfHoLT

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2022

However, the country has itself been experiencing growing levels of migration in recent years. Most of the new arrivals are from neighbouring Ukraine and Belarus, but there are also growing numbers from outside Europe, too.

Indians are now Poland’s third-largest immigrant group, numbering around 25,500, according to recent data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Among first residence permits issued by Poland last year, Indians (9,230) and Turks (7,533) were the fourth and fifth largest recipients.

Poland’s current government has blamed some immigrant groups for a rise in crime and has stepped up deportations of those found to have broken the law. However, data show that, overall, immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than Poles themselves.

]]> Polish police detain more teens following school knife attacks amid fears of further incidents https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/09/polish-police-detain-more-teens-following-school-knife-attacks-amid-fears-of-further-incidents/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 11:41:45 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105291

Following this week’s two knife attacks on schools in Poland, police have today carried out security checks on over 10,000 schools and detained at least 10 more people, many of them teenagers found to have made online threats or been in possession of weapons.

Meanwhile, many parents decided not to send their children to school today, as rumours swirled online that this week’s attacks were somehow coordinated and that further incidents were planned on Friday.

The issue has also sparked a political dispute, with the government criticising opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for previously vetoing laws intended to improve children’s safety. The opposition in turn accuses the government of failing to protect schools properly.

🚨 Ponad 10 tysięcy skontrolowanych placówek i 10 osób zatrzymanych w całym kraju.

Bezpieczeństwo w szkołach priorytetem Policji ⬇️

Tragiczne zdarzenia, do których doszło w ciągu ostatnich dni na Mazowszu, wywołały w przestrzeni medialnej falę nieprawdziwych informacji,… pic.twitter.com/WVkYUdVO9C

— Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) October 9, 2026

On Thursday, a 39-year-old school caretaker was killed in an attack by a 15-year-old former pupil on a primary school. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that the assailant had been wearing a head-mounted camera intended to broadcast the attack.

That came a day after a 19-year-old student carried out a knife attack on another school, leaving eight people injured. Two other teens were also detained on suspicion of planning attacks in other locations.

In response, Tusk announced on Thursday that police would carry out regular checks on schools. However, on Friday, many parents in the Masovia province around Warsaw, where both of this week’s attacks took place, decided to keep their children at home. Some districts closed schools entirely.

One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school by a 15-year-old former pupil.

Yesterday, a knife attack by a 19-year-old at another school left eight people injured. The assailant also had a homemade explosive that failed to detonate https://t.co/xJAzhT6u3U

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026

Concern was stoked by claims circulating on social media that this week’s school attacks were part of a coordinated action by a group of teenagers, who were planning further incidents on what they were calling “Bloody Friday”.

Two schools in the town of Legionowo, just north of Warsaw, were closed on Friday after local authorities said they received “unconfirmed information that they were on a list” relating to the alleged group.

Poland’s national police headquarters issued a statement on Friday morning saying that they were aware of the rumours but that “so far nothing indicates such an event is actually happening”. They urged people to remain calm, not share unverified information, and rely only on credible sources.

 

At the same time, police and local authorities stepped up security in schools. At 9 a.m. on Friday, the national police headquarters announced that checks had been conducted at over 10,000 schools around the country and that ten people had been detained.

Among those to be arrested was a 17-year-old in the town of Ełk, who had reportedly made online threats to attack other students, and a 13-year-old in Sochaczew who wrote in a chat that he would bring a machete to school. The boy later said it was a “silly joke”.

In Bartoszyce, a school principal saw that an 11-year-old student had posted a photo of a knife alongside a statement indicating a threat. Police detained the boy and found an “imitation knife” in his backpack.

In Ostrów Mazowiecka, police announced they had arrested a 15-year-old boy who had sent out images of himself in a Guy Fawkes-style mask, saying that he planned to take people’s lives. In Warsaw, police detained a 14-year-old who was found to be in possession of a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers.

🚨 Policjanci z Mokotowa niezwłocznie po otrzymaniu informacji o zagrożeniu bezpieczeństwa zatrzymali na terenie szkoły 14-latka, który posiadał nóż z ukrytym ostrzem. Nastolatek miał przy sobie także 11 petard hukowych.

W sprawie prowadzone są dalsze czynności. Dokumenty… pic.twitter.com/lbQrqe2pgl

— Policja Warszawa (@Policja_KSP) October 9, 2026

The situation has also taken on a political dimension. On Thursday, Tusk criticised Nawrocki for earlier this year vetoing a government bill intended to improve online safety by blocking harmful content. The president had argued that the measures were an “Orwellian” threat to free speech.

In a hastily called vote in the lower-house Sejm on Thursday evening, Tusk’s ruling coalition passed a new version of the bill that will now be sent to the upper-house Senate. Once it receives final parliamentary approval, the legislation will return to Nawrocki for his signature or veto.

Meanwhile, education minister Barbara Nowacka also noted that Nawrocki had vetoed a bill introducing new rights and responsibilities for school pupils, including greater powers to confiscate dangerous items.

💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️

Mieliśmy jedną z najmocniejszych propozycji zmiany prawa w Europie, która miała chronić w internecie przede wszystkim dzieci i młodzież. pic.twitter.com/dyxY6prGzB

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 8, 2026

In response, presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz criticised those who were “exploiting this issue for political purposes”, saying that “a political argument is the last thing we need right now”.

Meanwhile, Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of focusing on “political warfare” instead of ensuring security in schools.

“There is no coordination or top-down directives on what to do, where it is safe, and where there is risk or threat,” he wrote on social media, calling the situation “chaos”.

]]> Polish parliament approves ban on nighttime alcohol sales in shops https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/09/polish-parliament-approves-ban-on-nighttime-alcohol-sales-in-shops/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 08:46:35 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105280

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours.

The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved.

#PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6

— tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026

The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package.

The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently.

Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales.

In the first six months following the implementation of its restrictions in 2023, Kraków saw a nearly 50% decrease in nighttime police interventions, with other cities reporting similar improvements.

 

The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400).

Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage.

The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 zloty for stronger drinks.

Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops.

The new measure will come into force on 1 June 2026 and will apply from 10 p.m to 6 a.m. across the entire city https://t.co/A7xVvJMpvU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026

In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP).

The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment.

Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it.

Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, new data show.

The average person in Poland ate 82kg of meat last year, up 7.5% from 2024 and 22.7% since 2005.

They also drank 82 litres of beer, down 18.7% since 2018 https://t.co/FxFMupWLRv

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 1, 2026

In June, an IBRiS poll for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 55% of Poles support some form of ban on nighttime alcohol sales while 43% are opposed. A survey by IBP for Super Express published today showed even stronger support, with 67% in favour of a ban and only 26% opposed.

Recent data released by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, showed that alcohol consumption among Poles is continuing its recent decline.

In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019.

However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005.

]]> Polish man suspected of helping Russian plot to assassinate Zelensky sentenced to 5.5 years https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/08/polish-man-suspected-of-helping-russian-plot-to-assassinate-zelensky-sentenced-to-5-5-years/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:58:23 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105244

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.

The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding.

Sąd zaostrzył karę dla Pawła K. Chodzi o współpracę z rosyjskim wywiadem #lublin #szpieg #rosja #wywiad #wyrok https://t.co/Vg2zTx35l4

— Fakt (@Fakt_pl) October 8, 2026

The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024.

Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers.

Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine.

“These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year.

Poland and Ukraine have revealed further details of a foiled plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa at Poland's Rzeszów airport.

A Polish man was last month indicted in relation to the incident, which he is accused of seeking to carry out on behalf of Russia https://t.co/Lrp99vH4s2

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 23, 2025

Last year, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that Paweł K. had been “recruited decades ago and firmly believed in the Soviet cause”. Polish prosecutors have not commented on that claim.

However, they did find that the suspect had declared his willingness to join Russian “sabotage structures”, including the Wagner mercenary group and Unit 29155 of the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency, which is tasked with carrying out destabilisation activities.

Paweł G. denied the accusations against him and claimed that he had actually been trying to help capture Russian war criminals by deceiving them into trusting him, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

His defence attorney argued that the information Paweł G. had transmitted regarding Rzeszów airport was “trivial and publicly available”, according to news website Onet.

 

In January this year, Paweł K. was found guilty of espionage and illegal possession of ammunition by the district court in the city of Zamość, which sentenced him to three and a half years in prison.

However, prosecutors appealed against that ruling, arguing that the suspect deserved a longer jail term of seven and a half years. In a judgement issued on Thursday, the Lublin appeals court agreed that Paweł G’s initial sentence had been “grossly lenient” and increased it by two years, reports PAP.

“Submitting an offer to work for…the intelligence service of a country that is at war with a country directly neighboring Poland, a country that is making quite extensive unfriendly gestures towards Poland, cannot be treated leniently,” said judge Artur Achrymowicz.

Poland has charged three of its own citizens with working on behalf of Russian intelligence.

They are accused of spreading disinformation, conducting reconnaissance of NATO troops, and undergoing firearms training in preparation for acts of sabotage https://t.co/maYd0kb9HW

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 20, 2026

Poland has become a primary target for acts of espionage, sabotage and disinformation conducted by operatives working on behalf of Russia.

In many cases, they are so-called “disposable agents”: individuals already on the ground, often amateurs hired and paid through messaging apps such as Telegram, rather than professional spies or soldiers.

The AWB last year launched 48 investigations related to espionage, more than twice as many as in 2024. Over those two years, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined

A report published earlier this year by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe.

Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism.

Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026

In January, Polish prosecutors indicted five people – four Ukrainian citizens and one Russian – accused of carrying out a plot on behalf of Russia to plant explosives in packages that were then dispatched by courier services across Europe.

In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops.

A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it.

The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack.

“We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters.

“So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.”

Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000.

Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP.

However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down.

The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data.

The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013.

Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%.

The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030.

At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%).

After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU.

In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%).

And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%).

Meanwhile, both the number and proportion of women serving in the armed forces have increased dramatically. In 2015, there were only 4,000 professional female soldiers in Poland, a number that has now risen to almost 37,000.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Fri, 09 Oct 2026 21:11:13 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Investor pressure mounts on boss of King’s favourite interior designer https://www.cityam.com/pressure-mounts-on-boss-of-king-charles-favourite-interior-designer/ Sat, 10 Oct 2026 04:42:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464698

A former National Lottery boss is under growing pressure to quit as chair of King Charles’s preferred interior design outlet over opposition to the group’s “lavish” relocation and “poor performance”. Dame Dianne Thompson is facing calls to resign from her role at Sanderson Design Group as part of a campaign against the wallpaper company’s drift [...]]]>

A former National Lottery boss is under growing pressure to quit as chair of King Charles’s preferred interior design outlet over opposition to the group’s “lavish” relocation and “poor performance”.

Dame Dianne Thompson is facing calls to resign from her role at Sanderson Design Group as part of a campaign against the wallpaper company’s drift towards “inaction and inertia”. 

The design group’s history dates back more than a century and its Royal Warrant means the company’s fabrics and wall coverings adorn the official residences of the royal family. In February, the group launched a collection inspired by King Charles’s Highgrove Estate.

LBV Asset Management, which owns about 14 per cent of Sanderson, is pushing for Thompson to be removed as a director and chair. 

“This is by no means an indictment on Dame Thompson’s career or character, both of which are incredibly distinguished,” the investor told Sanderson last month.

“It is an indictment on the current state of the company, which requires leadership – and a chairman – with the mandate and sufficient tenure ahead of him or her to lead a sustained period of change.”

A number of shareholders in the Aim-listed firm, which is due to publish its half-year results on Monday, told City AM that they support LBV’s proposals, voicing a number of concerns over the group’s strategy. 

Paul Hawkins, an asset manager who holds a personal stake in the company, said that Sanderson’s “only excuse for poor performance always seems to come back to difficult economic conditions”. 

“That’s simply not good enough, especially when your biggest competitor in Colefax is performing well,” he added. 

Ex-lottery boss under pressure

Shareholders said that licensing revenue, which grew by a third to £9m in the year to January, is masking the firm’s wider underperformance. 

Hawkins said: “It makes no sense to me why Dame Diane Thompson wouldn’t bow out gracefully and accept it’s time to pass the baton onto someone new with fresh ideas and challenge to a management team that clearly needs it.”

Sanderson is in the midst of a turnaround under chief executive Lisa Montague. The firm posted a £3m pre-tax profit in the year to January, up from a £14m loss the previous year.

But LBV has criticised the board’s decision to approve Montague’s £729,000 pay packet for this year. Her total pay deal, combined with that of Sanderson’s finance chief, accounted to 36 per cent of the group’s profit.

“They are being paid extremely well to repair the profitability that has fallen so considerably under their watch. The Chair doesn’t appear to have a credible answer as to why this is justified,” Hawkins said.

Shareholders expressed concern over Sanderson’s recent relocation to Voysey House, a Grade II-listed building in Chiswick, west London.

One shareholder who is close to the firm’s senior management told City AM that the move to the site of the interior designer’s former factory was a “vanity project” and a “poor use of shareholder funds”.

They said: “Everyone in the industry is at Chelsea Harbour, but Sanderson, at a time of extremely poor performance, decided to relocate to Voysey House.” Another shareholder criticised the “expensive” relocation.

Rhys Summerton, the founder of Milkwood Capital, told City AM that the upgrades to Voysey House ahead of the company’s move were “lavishly done,” though he said it makes sense for the firm to be at its “historical home”. 

A spokesperson for Sanderson said: “Voysey House has been Sanderson Design Group’s spiritual home for more than 100 years. 

“It is central to unlocking the commercial value of our 75,000-piece archive, bringing together our design teams and providing a hub for global customer engagement and partnerships.”

Sanderson ‘neglected by shareholders’

Shareholders said Sanderson has been slow to expand in the US market, where Aim-listed competitor Colefax has toasted an “exceptionally strong sales performance”.

“In my view the business and its leadership need to have much greater focus on their core UK market. They have a wide distribution that they are directly in control of,” the person close to Sanderson’s management said.

“Whilst overseas markets, particularly the US, and licensing are important, they alone will not resolve Sanderson’s problems.”

Summerton said Milkwood has backed LBV’s proposals because Sanderson needs more oversight. “The governance that you see at Sanderson is very similar to the governance that you see at a lot of other smaller companies,” Summerton said.

“Shareholders neglect the company and the decision-making sometimes and the scrutiny of the executives, and that results in underperformance.”

A person close to LBV said that the investor has never taken such direct action with a company before. “They are not an aggressive player in that way but this time they feel they had no choice.”

Sanderson’s history dates back to 1860, when Athur Sanderson & Sons was founded in Islington. In 1940, the designer bought Morris & Co, the brand founded by Arts and Crafts pioneer William Morris. 

The company’s spokesperson added: “The Board firmly believes neither of LBV’s proposed resolutions are in the best interests of the Company and its shareholders. 

“Immediate removal of the Chair would risk unnecessary disruption at a time when the Group’s strategy is delivering measurable progress and profitability, and the Board does not consider that LBV has demonstrated how its nominee’s appointment would strengthen the Company.

“Our focus remains on delivering sustained profitable growth and shareholder value. We will set out our full response to both resolutions in the forthcoming shareholder circular.”

]]> 2464698Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Bagatelle: Is exclusive Chelsea offering future of Premier League hospitality? https://www.cityam.com/bagatelle-is-exclusive-chelsea-offering-future-of-premier-league-hospitality/ Sat, 10 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2463893

Bagatelle has opened inside Chelsea’s Stamford Bridge. Matt Hardy went down to see if it lives up to its reputation. It feels like every week a top football club opens a new hospitality offering that claims to reinvent what has, in reality, long been the status quo: a good bit of food and a free [...]]]>

Bagatelle has opened inside Chelsea’s Stamford Bridge. Matt Hardy went down to see if it lives up to its reputation.

It feels like every week a top football club opens a new hospitality offering that claims to reinvent what has, in reality, long been the status quo: a good bit of food and a free bar.

That changed, pretty dramatically, when Fulham opened their Riverside Stand with its £20,000 season tickets, Michelin-starred chefs and tidal wave of cocktails.

City AM was told that this offering – seen as one of the best across the Premier League’s 20 clubs – had been topped in another corner of south west London. So, naturally, we had to investigate.

If you were to search for Bagatelle on TikTok just a few months ago you’d have been met with youngsters – 20 to 40 somethings – in Saint-Tropez trying their very best to enjoy themselves in the sweaty French summer.

Do the same search today and you’ll find a very similar clientele – only inside Chelsea’s Stamford Bridge instead.

Bagatelle describes itself as a “French hospitality brand of luxury restaurants and beach clubs”. So why has it gone into football, and why Chelsea?

Bagatelle… at Chelsea?

“Chelsea are world champions, they’re known around the world, they sit in probably the most affluent postcode in sports,” Bagatelle International co-founder Salima Vellani tells City AM.

“Moving into sports was kind of the new flex for us in terms of where the brand is going – it’s more of a luxury lifestyle platform, not just a restaurant group.

“We know where our clients want us to be and so we’re moving in that direction. And sports is missing this layer and it’s never been done in Premier League football.”

The 80-cover offering is, frankly, a little odd. As a sports fan you wouldn’t have known you were at one of the capital’s great sporting arenas. As a Chelsea fan – which the lady next to me was – it may borderline on infuriating.

Getting a ticket at Chelsea is difficult as it is, especially with a number of seats being converted from general admission to hospitality. But Vellani rightly points out that they have instead taken seats away from other premium areas of the ground, rather than general admission.

“I have a brand that I have to protect,” she says. “What I don’t want to do is go in and fit into your box. What I need is [that] you fit into our vision.

“[Chelsea] and Legends, which operates the stadium, are phenomenal partners, they agreed to do it and said, ‘Let’s create something totally different that’s never been seen before’.

“I wanted to create a new category. We’ve been pioneers in the restaurant space, let’s be pioneers in the sports space. I saw a gap, and that gap is luxury VIP hospitality as opposed to what they call premium.”

The reality

What Bagatelle at Stamford Bridge is, however, is perfectly designed for a specific group of people; those who want to experience football their own way. 

Vellani says the offering has been popular with women; at last month’s Hull City game the clientele was predominantly female. 

She says it allows players, their partners and high-level guests to relax. John Terry, harassed for a picture only once or twice, certainly looked at ease.

It has a place in football, and those who hate that may not quite understand how the game has evolved. The food – ranging from tuna tartare to steak to full-time pizzas – was exceptional. The booze – often prescriptive in these settings – was plentiful and wide-ranging.

Bagatelle is known for its party atmosphere, and the Stamford Bridge opening was no different. Waiters stood on chairs singing, lights flickered on, off and on again, and everyone was encouraged to get involved. 

Singing Titanic theme My Heart Will Go On mere minutes before Chelsea saw an early Morgan Rogers goal sunk by two Hull efforts in a 2-2 draw was perhaps not the best example of foreshadowing.

The partnership stems from Chelsea’s deal with Legends – a venue management firm – and Vellani, who said Bagatelle is launching a country club concept and also heading into the boutique hotels market, explains that while this is their first club, it may not be their last.

State of the sport

“We’re partnering with Legends,” she says. “We’re having massive conversations with them and we hope to take this around the world – not only to other clubs in the UK, but the US and further afield. 

“What we don’t want to do is be in a 100 sports stadiums, because that takes away from the brand. We want to be very selective in which ones we go into and Legends are very supportive of that, and actually have recognised that there is a whole new tier of sports hospitality that has gone amiss.

“British sports fans have been very true to the sport. American fans have been very true to the experience and the environment, but Legends have said they haven’t seen this in the US either.”

The reality is the football is changing, fan demands are evolving and clubs are constantly seeking new ways to drive up their top line. That may be an uncomfortable truth for many, but a truth nonetheless.

In Bagatelle’s Stamford Bridge offering – upwards of £1,000 per head – you see hospitality goers turfed out to make room for hospitality goers. It’s like-for-like and that’s perfectly reasonable. 

What you get from the experience, meanwhile, is like nothing else in the Premier League. It’s not premium; it’s luxury. It is finding its place in modern football, and it is, frankly, an exceptional way to spend a couple of hours on a Saturday afternoon. 

]]> 2463893Matt Hardy Matt Hardy Number 10 launches aviation charm offensive after Burnham third runway remarks https://www.cityam.com/number-10-calms-aviation-sector-nerves-over-third-runway-fears/ Sat, 10 Oct 2026 03:47:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464666

Andy Burnham’s Downing Street operation has been privately reassuring members of the aviation sector of its support for Heathrow’s third runway expansion, despite the Prime Minister refusing to give the megaproject his backing in a string of media appearances over Labour party conference. City AM understands that Number 10 has been trying to patch up [...]]]>

Andy Burnham’s Downing Street operation has been privately reassuring members of the aviation sector of its support for Heathrow’s third runway expansion, despite the Prime Minister refusing to give the megaproject his backing in a string of media appearances over Labour party conference.

City AM understands that Number 10 has been trying to patch up relations with key figures from the industry after many were left disoriented by the former Manchester mayor’s indifference towards the multibillion-pound drive at his party’s annual jamboree last week. Government advisers have assured the sector that the remarks were not a sign of government going cold on the project, three industry figures said, and that Burnham had not been fully briefed on its economic merits.

“Andy Burnham’s comments weren’t necessarily helpful at the time – but we’ve had some clarification since,” one exec said. “No 10 and internal advisers basically told us the Prime Minister hadn’t really had the time to focus on aviation and the runway. One has to recognise that… his father died [and] he was busy preparing for conference. Aviation was probably the last thing on his mind.”

Proponents of the third runway had initially been encouraged that the change in Prime Minister would not herald any cooling of appetite for the third runway, after Burnham handed aviation minister Keir Mather a brief that explicitly included oversight of Heathrow expansion. Heathrow boss Thomas Woldbye has also said Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, gave the project his blessing when the pair first spoke in July.

Third runway bidders gear up for pivotal evidence session

But their confidence in the project was thrown into disarray when Burnham, who as Manchester mayor called for the third runway plans to be abandoned, told the BBC the expansion was “a matter for London and Londoners”. “I think it’s right that we hear what people have said through the consultation, and then then consider the way forward from there,” he said in an interview ahead of Labour’s conference.

The remarks stood in sharp contrast to the four square support that Keir Starmer gave the runway throughout his time in office. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves made it a central plank of her mission to fire up the UK economy, saying the country could not “duck the decision any longer” in a speech last year that fired the starting gun on its lengthy planning process.

Officials are currently wading their way through responses to a consultation on the Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement, which when published will act as a framework against which bidders’ planning applications will be judged. Civil servants will then unveil a final version of the document, which will be put to a vote now expected in early next year.

Flights by 2039?

If passed, owner Heathrow Airport Limited (HAL) is expected to submit a proposal alongside Heathrow West, a rival bid that is being spearheaded by the billionaire hotel tycoon Surinder Arora. Transport secretary Heidi Alexander will then consider the applications before deciding which, if any, the government should rubber stamp.

But the project has already been dealt its first major blow when HAL conceded it was unlikely to hit its initial 2035 target for flights to take off from the strip. It now expects to deliver the expansion by 2039, assuming the planning process remains on track.

Separately, HAL boss Woldbye and Arora are gearing up for a pivotal evidence session at Transport Committee this week, where MPs are expected to grill the pair on the the merits of expansion and their proposals. Critics argue that even if costs are kept to a minimum, passengers will have to foot the vast majority of the bill via charges that are added to their plane tickets.

A Department for Transport spokeswoman said: “Heathrow expansion has the potential to deliver around £40bn in economic benefits across the UK, and we support airport expansion across the country where this can contribute to growth and opportunity, while meeting tests on the environment.

“We are moving swiftly to review the responses received to the recent consultation on the policy framework underpinning expansion, and considering the appropriate next steps.”

]]> 2464666Ali Lyon Ali Lyon Inherit film review: Thai horror explores society’s Faustian pact https://www.cityam.com/inherit-film-review-thai-horror-explores-societys-faustian-pact/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 17:33:48 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464722

Thai horror Inherit skewers youth obsession with slick scares, Buddhist exorcism and a vampish demon grandma; read why its satire endures.]]>

Inherit | Dir. Banjong Pisanthanakun | ★★★★☆

Our obsession with looking – and remaining – young is stretched to its horrifying logical conclusion in slick Thai horror film Inherit. 

The Manasvanich family is in crisis over a chemical leak at their factory, which may or may not be causing birth defects in the local population: the last thing they need is an unexpected visit from a long-lost octogenarian relative. But when Grandma Woranart turns up, she is no little old lady – she’s a bombshell in eveningwear who makes everyone both horny and uncomfortable. 

“Grandma”, as this seemingly twentysomething woman insists on being called, appears to have found the elixir of youth. What’s her secret? Botox? GLP-1s? Chemical peels? Sure, all of those, she says with a sultry smile. The family’s teenage daughter Oui strikes up a particularly firm friendship with Grandma, lounging with her beside the pool and going on girlie shopping trips, only slightly perturbed by the string of violent deaths that follow in her wake.

It doesn’t take long for everyone to realise that Grandma has sold her soul to an ageless centipede demon, and soon the chase is afoot: can the Manasvaniches exorcise this evil spirit before she claims another vessel – and will this secretive family survive intact?

For Western audiences, part of Inherit’s charm is seeing a familiar trope – demons being battled by religious types – shifted to another culture. Priests bearing crucifixes are replaced by robed monks and icons of the Virgin Mary become statues of the Buddha.

Inherit sees Banjong Pisanthanakun on top form

We must cherish the live sport offering in Britain and celebrate what it gives us, writes Pitch Experiences chief Neil Bailey.

As the festive season approaches, hospitality bigwigs get down to business: the wine list, cocktails and menu are tweaked; the music is mixed for the crowd and even the big moments are designed to make everyone feel special on the day.

Yes, shaping hospitality at today’s big sporting events is increasingly a bit like being a wedding planner. Everything is curated to create talkability, shareability and – sorry to use this phrase – to make memories. It is what sport has become, something people demand more from.

We’ve seen a shift across the hospitality sector already this year; the demand for the major events is bigger than ever. Whether at Allianz Stadium, Wembley, Alexandra Palace or Silverstone, the mega-moment occasions are what’s driving the industry. And that in turn is driving a change in experience demands.

Sporting schedule expands

The ever-growing sporting fixture schedule appears to be causing City corporate spending to focus on the tier one events. Rather than spread the hospitality pound over a series of occasions – such as a season-long box – clients are focused on the elite sporting moments in the calendar. With that switch in focus comes a need to make each one count. Amalgamating all the elements to make the day as special as it can be is the difficult bit.

Sport seems to increase in popularity year-on-year, and the cachet of attending a major sporting event has never been so high. You may be able to see highlights, clips and chat immediately online, but nothing hits quite like being able to say “I was there”. Other than perhaps being able to remind somebody, “I invited you there”.

The desire to attend and host colleagues and clients at the biggest of games means that some of the mainstream events need to work harder to be the draw they once were. World Rugby has innovated to create the Nations’ Championship and the finals weekend at Twickenham is already proving to be popular with Pitch Experiences in the run-up to the Men’s Rugby World Cup next season. The promise of several matches, northern hemisphere vs southern hemisphere clashes, world ranking points and a trophy at the end of it means that it’s more attractive than the usual autumn internationals series that was played until this season. Fans want to see competition and occasions which truly mean something.

Hospitality the way?

Despite a degree of backlash over ticket prices, bookings for next year’s Ashes are well ahead of expectations. With ticket prices in line with other major sporting events and well below some such as the recent football World Cup – albeit staged in the more commercialised North American market – cricket should be proud that we have a summer-long event that draws the crowds, no matter what. What’s better than a 10-hour sporting hospitality day, after all?

Corporate hospitality at sport may have been unforgettable in the past because of the amount of booze on offer. Those boisterous “boys’ days out” are now long gone, however; at today’s events the wine list gets genuine attention, as do the selection of non-alcoholic beers and mocktails.

But what have we realised fans want, besides a slap up meal and a fancy cocktail or a nice bottle of red? Sports punditry is everywhere on our many screens and seeing the same old names from the past is often just background noise. We’re increasingly involving today’s players in our pre-match build up. Those injured or out of the matchday squad can provide fascinating tactical and technical insight that you can’t get anywhere else. It makes the audience feel in-the-know and ahead of the game.

Change of pace

We’ve also seen a positive reaction to inviting sports industry executives along to chat with guests. You may not like a change in format in cricket or rugby, but nowhere else can you ask the people behind it about it.

We probably don’t celebrate enough the incredible sporting calendar we have here, instead focusing on rules, regulations and ticket accessibility. But we should be unapologetic about what this nation offers its sports fans, and that includes hospitality too – Formula 1 and the British Grand Prix proves that curating experiences to a domestic audience can be top tier. People want to be part of it and an iconic venue resonates with a global audience.

So we should continue to back our Britishness by going to the best events, whether in the rafters or the padded seats.

Into the Woods by Stephen Sondheim review and star rating: ★★★

Musical theatre can be self-referential, didn’t you know? Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine certainly do. Their Into The Woods maxes out on meta gameplay in this technically brilliant but at times baseless musical that can be terribly proud of itself.

A baker and his wife plunge into Tom Scutt’s endless-feeling set, which is in effect a handful of trees and some carefully placed reeds but feels immensely lush and escapist, in order to break the spell that forbids them from having children. They must venture into the woods to bring back four items: a cow as white as milk, a cape as red as blood, hair as yellow as corn, and a slipper as pure as gold, says a familiar-looking witch, and Cinderella, Little Red Riding Hood, Jack from Jack and the Beanstalk are along for the ride too (don’t ask). 

Into the Woods: London return is technically spectacular

As for the music, it’s no surprise that Cinderella and Little Red Riding Hood have whooping great belts; it’s all technically spectacular and the music relieving because, frankly, Lapine’s script is often mercilessly verbose, overflowing with narrative information about the side quests of each of the characters. By the end of the first act it appears to be a fun, big-hearted journey, and musically triumphant, and everyone gets what they wish for, babies are due and it’s all gravy – but there is a second act in which everything falls apart again when a new plot is introduced: a vengeful giant is on the loose.

I’d imagine the Venn diagram of Stephen Sondheim and Brothers Grimm fans is fairly robust, but the conceit starts to feel like intellectual masturbation by the second act. After all, the viewer has no cliffhanger to resolve after the interval, which itself feels longer than other shows (I don’t know if this was intentional, or if there was a production issue on the night I went in). Anyway, returning to my seat after a lengthy first act, and due to the fast-paced, sometimes overwhelming narrative, I was wearying of this forest-dwelling gang, a feeling I found hard to shake even with the arrival of the eventual fee-fi-fo-fum thuds of the worrisome vertically accomplished beast edging ever closer.

Tunes aren’t gripping

The other problem with Into the Woods is that there’s a lack of conventionally melodic pop songs to tide you over. The main refrain – into the wooooooodsssssss – is repeated a thousand times, and is unconventionally catchy, but not in the rewarding way of something more tuneful. The metaness bleeds through from the staging into the ballads: everyone’s belting something for the sake of musical theatre, darling, but perhaps when everyone’s belting, no one’s belting at all. 

I don’t want to diminish the innovative brilliance of this expansive idea, which genuinely transports you somewhere fairytale-coded and magical looking. Call me Scrooge (one of a  few fictional characters who doesn’t get a look in) but I suppose you could argue that the virtue of fairy tales is that they end quickly. There is energy and wonder here, though I left a little exhausted.

Into the Woods plays at the Noël Coward Theatre until 9 January 2027

Retaining the individuals who allocate capital and fund business expansion should be considered a national priority, but Healey looks more likely to drive them away, writes Tom Goddard

Financial professionals have the resources to leave the UK if they feel unfairly targeted by tax rises, or that the tax they pay is not spent wisely by the government. By increasing taxes such as Capital Gains Tax (CGT) or dividend tax in the Autumn Budget, the Chancellor John Healey could be sacrificing long-term, high-value tax contributions for a short-term fiscal gain.

The top 10 per cent of taxpayers in the UK contribute 60 per cent of total income tax receipts. Private equity houses and venture capital firms directly generate approximately £200bn of the UK’s GDP, representing around seven per cent of economic output, and support more than 2.5m jobs, all of whom will pay income tax and National Insurance Contributions (NICs).

London remains one of the world’s premier financial centres. Alongside New York, it is one of only a handful of genuinely global hubs for financial services, private capital and asset management. It possesses a unique ecosystem comprising world-class legal services, deep capital markets, leading universities, a highly skilled workforce and an abundance of financial expertise. The government should recognise this as a national strength that can attract and retain global talent and focus on promoting its growth rather than treating it as a bottomless well for ever-higher taxation.

Healey must think longer term

When senior investment professionals choose to locate in London, they bring with them whole networks of advisers and businesses. They deploy capital into British businesses, support entrepreneurial ventures and create opportunities for future generations of founders and employees. The compounding effect generated by these industries has helped make London Europe’s dominant financial centre, which ultimately leads to larger tax hauls.

The danger is that when a senior financial executive relocates away from the UK, this wider supporting network of professionals may also leave. Although London’s success as a financial hub is not based on the UK’s tax regime, it is not immune from competition from other jurisdictions able to capitalise on the flow of professionals and businesses from the UK, which eventually, may weaken the same ecosystem that made the UK attractive in the first place.

Healey’s approach should therefore be one of strategic competitiveness and continued growth. Rather than viewing successful investors and entrepreneurs primarily as a source of additional tax revenue, the government should recognise them as drivers of economic activity whose presence generates investment, employment and innovation throughout the wider economy.

The UK is in competition with several countries that are actively seeking to attract internationally mobile wealth creators through favourable tax regimes. Greece, Italy, Portugal, Switzerland and the UAE have all developed frameworks designed to appeal to entrepreneurs, investors and senior financial executives. Their objective is to attract high earners who generate tax revenue, invest capital, create jobs and support economic growth.

At a time when economic growth remains the government’s primary challenge, retaining the individuals who allocate capital and fund business expansion should be considered a national priority and the UK must ensure that it remains not only a great place to invest, but also a great place for investors to live, work and build their businesses.

Tom Goddard is an assistant manager at Blick Rothenberg

You know something is wrong with the upper end of Britain’s labour market when some of the country’s most promising companies find it is easier to relocate top talent from America than hire from our own shores.

But those are exactly the lengths to which one founder told me he and his fellow UK tech entrepreneurs are regularly going to take on high-skilled engineers quick enough to fuel their companies’ rapid growth.

The rise in this sub-optimal practice is not, you will be relieved to read, for a lack of high-functioning, high-IQ minds being churned out by our universities.

The culprit, in fact, is the thicket of draconian, anticompetitive clauses that employers are minded to slap on the contracts of their brightest and best.

Speaking to City AM’s Saskia Koopman last month, Fuse Energy boss Alan Chang lamented the practice as “another barrier to building generational companies here”. The upshot, he said, is that his energy disruptor, and the country as a whole, can’t grow as quickly as they otherwise might.

Well, this morning, Andy Burnham and his business secretary Jonathan Reynolds have heeded those warnings – and not a moment too soon. During a speech in his spiritual home of Manchester, he vowed to clamp down on pesky non-compete agreements and lengthy notice periods in a move that should inject a bit of much-needed dynamism into the upper end of the UK’s jobs ecosystem.

Are non-competes preventing the next Revolut?

I make no apologies when I say that the issue of excessively long non-competes has become something of a cause celebre for City AM over the past few months.

And the rationale for that is quite simple. Sadly, Britain can’t claim to be genuinely world-leading in many corners of industry in today’s hypercompetitive global economy. But one bright pocket where we can go toe-to-toe against pretty much anyone is… brains. Few places, if anywhere, can lay claim to the volume of scarily clever people that currently reside in the ‘golden triangle’ between London, Oxford and Cambridge.

Just the other day, I was speaking to a fascinating founder called Alex Fitzgerald (full profile of him and his company Isembard to follow next week) who hailed London and the South East as “the best place in the world” to find manufacturing engineers, robotics engineers and software engineers in one place. Not to mention the legal, marketing and sales gurus also needed to run his high-precision manufacturing firm. In America, by comparison, that talent is spread out across many of their sprawling 50 states.

And yet, because of arcane and anachronistic employment practices, in the UK, we have failed to capitalise fully on the nascent potential that talent holds. People with brains the size of Mars – ready to build the next Revolut – are often hamstrung from doing so because their contract at a big bank or hedge fund prevents it. Just as common, are the mind-bogglingly long notice periods to which top talent are held: do we really want individuals who, single-handedly, produce millions of pounds-worth of economic activity a single month to be idling around on gardening leave for over a year?

For those who care deeply about the health and dynamism of the UK economy, there has been no shortage of underwhelming announcements to come from the early days of Burnham’s premiership. Today’s move on anti-competitive non-competes, however, should be cheered.

Rent musical review and star rating: ★★★

It’s pertinently ironic that Rent’s press night coincided with the London Film Festival premiere of Elsinore, Andrew Scott’s remarkably tender AIDS drama. Perhaps in the late-eighties when this musical was conceived, even talking about the epidemic on a stage was politically powerful, even if it were sprinkled as a theme rather than addressed head-on like dramas do today. 

By those standards, Jonathan Larson’s Rent, which follows a group of creatives fighting eviction from their New York building, was once fearsomely progressive. But by today’s standards, taking something so horrific as AIDS, which took the lives of 20,000 Brits alone, and putting it as a backdrop to a central story about people getting kicked out of their flats (which is dealt with with far more emotion) feels strange and tone deaf.

Rent musical: go for the music

In act 2 there is one attempt to go beyond two-dimensional representation with the platforming of the death of one character, Angel, to the disease, which is treated with more sensitivity via the track I’ll Cover You, but this production lets down the attempt: dressed in y-fronts and disappearing within sheets, Angel’s death feels bizarre and emotionless rather than profound.

Regardless, the pop-rock songs are fun, most notably Seasons of Love, famous more recently from Glee, even if many are strangely buoyant given they’re often about dying and how many of the characters have the disease.

If Rent is for one thing, it is taking in these spectacular songbooks, which includes bangers like La Vie Bohème, One Song Glory and Take Me Or Leave Me. A former City trader previously convicted of rigging the Euribor interest rates has had his fraud conviction overturned.

Christian Bittar, formerly a trader at Deutsche Bank, had his conviction overturned by the Court of Appeal on Friday after being sentenced to five years in prison for rigging the primary European interest rate, the Euro Interbank Offered Rate (Euribor), in the run-up to the financial crisis. He previously pleaded guilty to the charge.

“For reasons we will set out at a later date, this conviction has been quashed,” Lord Justice Edis told the court.

The decision comes just over a year after the Supreme Court’s landmark decision to overturn a similar ruling on former UBS trader Tom Hayes and Carlo Palombo, formerly of Barclays, last year, after finding they had been “deprived” of a fair trial as the judges had given “inaccurate and unfair” directions to the juries which found the traders guilty.

The two former City traders became the faces of the so-called ‘Libor scandal’ which saw the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) pursue a volley of prosecutions in the wake of the 2008 crash.

However, in Bittar’s appeal, he claimed he had pleaded guilty on the wrong legal basis, and brought his appeal after the Supreme Court overturned Hayes’ and Palombo’s convictions.

Speaking after the hearing, Hayes told City AM: “I’m overwhelmed because it’s been a long, long journey, and I’ve been fighting for all of us, not just me.

“The fact that now somebody who pleaded guilty has had their conviction deemed unsafe by the Court of Appeal is a huge step towards correcting all the injustices that took place in this series of cases,” he added.

The latest decision comes after five former City traders, Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon and Colin Bermingham, previously convicted of rigging the Libor (London Interbank Offered Rate) and Euribor interest rates had their fraud convictions overturned by the Court of Appeal on Wednesday, all of whom pleaded not guilty.

The five investment bankers, who previously worked at Barclays, had their convictions quashed having served jail-time for conspiring to rig the now-defunct Libor interest rates in the run-up to the financial crisis.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) referred the cases to the court in January after the fraud watchdog, which brought the prosecutions over a decade ago, said it would not seek a retrial against Hayes and Palombo.

“I have waited a very, very long time for this day. Finally, the injustice of what I and others suffered has been recognised. I am so grateful for those who stood by me through this ordeal and those who worked so tirelessly to correct it,” Bittar commented after the hearing.

Ben Rose, of Hickman and Rose, representing Bittar, said it “is significant that the Court of Appeal today quashed Christian’s conviction in face of opposition from the SFO.” 

“The decision to quash Christian’s guilty plea illustrates the severity of the injustice he suffered. Courts are naturally reluctant to set aside guilty pleas, so I am delighted that the Court of Appeal agreed that, exceptionally, it should do so in this case,” Rose said.

“It is a scandal that the SFO has consistently failed to uphold its duty to seek to ensure that these trials are fair. It is hard to see how it will learn the lessons it needs to of this saga until it accepts it was wrong,” he said.

‘The last chapter’ in the rates-rigging scandal

Bittar is the last of the group of former traders who have had their appeals heard.

“Some of us lived that history. It’s quite something to be here today in the last chapter of it,” Bittar’s barrister told the court.

However, the ninth and last former trader who was pursued by the SFO, Peter Johnson, formerly of Barclays and the original whistleblower in the rates-rigging scandal, is in the early stages of an appeal, Lord Justice Edis confirmed to the court on Friday. Like Bittar, Johnson also pled guilty, and was sentenced to four years in prison.

“The quashing of these convictions is welcome news and another important step on the way to correcting this terrible miscarriage of justice,” Ellen Gallagher, partner at Vardags, who represents Johnson, said. 

“But Peter’s fight to clear his name continues, and he intends to appeal. As the Court made clear today, he has taken the first steps towards that appeal by filing provisional grounds. 

“We await the Court’s fully reasoned decision on this week’s appeals and are considering next steps,” Gallagher said.

Jason Williams, head of division at the SFO said in a statement: “We argued for a different outcome but respect the court’s decision in relation to Christian Bittar. The SFO remains committed to tackling the most complex fraud, bribery and corruption.”

Deutsche Bank declined to comment.
